pool.q: What pathologic finding characterizes sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) and can distinguish SO from Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome?

options.a: diffuse nongranulomatous inflammation involving the choriocapillaris
options.b: diffuse granulomatous inflammation involving the choriocapillaris
options.c: diffuse nongranulomatous inflammation sparing the choriocapillaris
options.d: diffuse granulomatous inflammation sparing the choriocapillaris

pool.rationale: Sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) is a granulomatous panuveitis that occurs after accidental or surgical trauma to 1 eye, followed by later inflammatory reaction of the fellow eye. Whereas the choriocapillaris is classically uninvolved in early SO, VKH typically involves the entire choroid/choriocapillaris.

pool.q: Medulloepitheliomas of the ciliary body develop from what tissue?
pool.rationale: Medulloepithelioma is a rare tumor of the ciliary body, and rarely retina or optic nerve, that is composed of neuroepithelial cells derived from primitive medullary epithelium (the inner layer of the optic cup) (figures). This congenital tumor is usually seen in children 4-12 years old. There are rare reports of medulloepithelioma in adults. The tumor appears as a cystic ciliary body mass that may erode into the iris root and anterior chamber. Rarely secondary glaucoma, hyphema, and ectopia lentis may occur. Pathologically, the tumor shows ribbons and cords of primitive round and oval cells, forming multiple layers of neuroepithelial tubules lined by a thin basement membrane. A primitive vitreous-like material composed of hyaluronic acid is secreted on one surface. The neuroblastic cells are similar in appearance to the cells of retinoblastoma. Mucinous cysts and Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes may be seen. Medulloepitheliomas may demonstrate heteroplastic tissue from several germ layers, such as cartilage or smooth muscle, and are termed teratoid medulloepitheliomas. Rarely medulloepitheliomas have large numbers of undifferentiated cells, mitotic figures, and evidence of tissue invasion, and are termed "malignant," although the course is usually benign if enucleation is performed before orbital invasion.

pool.q: What cell type does retinoblastoma originate from?
pool.rationale:
Retinoblastoma was once thought to be of glial origin, and tumors simulating retinoblastoma were referred to as "pseudogliomas," but the neuroblastic origin of retinoblastoma from nucleated layers of the retina is now well established.
Retinoblastoma does not originate from epithelial or mesenchymal cells.

pool.q: What histologic finding is associated with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome?
pool.rationale: Dalen-Fuchs nodules are collections of epithelioid histiocytes and lymphocytes between Bruch membrane and the RPE. They can be seen in sympathetic ophthalmia and ­Vogt-­Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome. In VKH syndrome, the entire choroid, including the choriocapillaris, is typically involved by the inflammatory process; relative sparing of the choriocapillaris is characteristic of sympathetic ophthalmia. Fundus autofluorescence and optic nerve head atrophy are not usually associated with VKH syndrome.

pool.q: What is the order in which the 3 phases of wound repair occur?
pool.rationale:
The purpose of wound healing is to restore the anatomical and functional integrity of an organ or tissue. There are 3 stages to wound healing:
  • The acute inflammatory phase, which may last from minutes to hours. Blood clots quickly in adjacent vessels in response to tissue activators. Neutrophils and fluid enter the extravascular space. Macrophages remove debris from the damaged tissues, new vessels form, and fibroblasts begin to produce collagen.
  • Regeneration, the replacement of lost cells, occurs only in tissues composed of cells capable of undergoing mitosis throughout life (eg, epithelial cells, fibroblasts). Repair is the process of restructuring of tissues that leads to a fibrous scar.
  • Contraction is the final phase; the reparative tissues start to shrink so that the scar is smaller than the surrounding uninjured tissues.
Infection is a complication of wound healing. Scarification is a confounding term that means scratching. Although ""retraction" means "the act of withdrawing" and could be used as a substitute for "contraction," it is not regularly used in wound-healing terminology.

pool.q: An Asian patient presents with a recent history of bilateral uveitis with hearing disturbance complaining of poor vision. She has been told nothing can be done to improve her vision and comes for a second opinion. There are yellow-white subretinal scars in her fundus. What was the most likely diagnosis at the time of her active disease?
pool.rationale:
Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome occurs most commonly in people with Asian, Asian Indian, Hispanic, Native American, and Middle Eastern ancestry. There are 4 stages: prodromal, acute uveitic, convalescent, and chronic recurrent. This patient likely described having the prodromal and acute uveitic phases in her past. The prodromal stage is marked by flulike symptoms. Auditory problems are observed in 75% of patients and frequently coincide with the onset of ocular disease. Central dysacusia, generally involving higher frequencies or tinnitus, affects 30% of patients early in the disease course, typically improving within 2-3 months; however, persistent deficits may remain. The acute uveitic stage is characterized by sequential blurring of vision in both eyes, 1-2 days after the onset of neurological symptoms, with bilateral granulomatous anterior uveitis, varying degrees of vitritis, thickening of the posterior choroid, optic nerve edema and multiple serous retinal detachments. Several weeks later, the exudative retinal detachments resolve and gradual depigmentation of the choroid occurs, leading to the classic sunset-glow fundus. Integumentary changes (perilimbal vitiligo [Sugiura sign], vitiligo, alopecia, poliosis) occur during the convalescent stage. The chronic recurrent stage is characterized by recurrent bouts of granulomatous anterior uveitis, which may occur concomitantly with subclinical choroidal inflammation requiring systemic therapy. Visually debilitating sequelae of chronic inflammation develop during this last stage; they include posterior subcapsular cataract, glaucoma, CNV, and subretinal fibrosis. The fundus exam in this patient most likely revealed subretinal fibrosis. These changes have not been described in sympathetic ophthalmia. Susac syndrome is associated with hearing loss but does not have the retinal findings described. Instead, fundus exam reveals diffuse or localized narrowing of retinal arteries with a “boxcar” segmentation. Subretinal fibrosis and uveitis is an uncommon panuveitis syndrome of unknown etiology with bilateral white-yellow lesions in the posterior pole that either fade without retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) alterations, become atrophic, or enlarge and coalesce into large, white, stellate zones of subretinal fibrosis. It is not associated with auditory disturbances.
The figures show various findings associated with different phases of VKH. Note also, the diagnosis of VKH requires bilateral involvement and the absence of penetrating ocular injury and other ocular or systemic disease. Cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis initially. Topical and systemic steroids are the first line of therapy, with immunosuppressants for recurrent or resistant cases.
Figure 1: Color fundus photographs (A, B) and late fluorescein angiograms (C, D) showing bilateral exudative retinal detachments with early peripapillary and extrafoveal subretinal fibrosis. Late fluorescein angiograms demonstrate numerous punctate hyperfluorescent leaks at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium, late filling of serous retinal detachment spaces, and variable blockage and staining of areas of subretinal fibrosis. Vision was hand motion in the right eye and 20/400 in the left eye.
Figure 2: Color fundus photographs (A, B) and late fluorescein angiograms (C, D) of same patient, 1 year after referral showing resolved exudative retinal detachments, widespread retinal pigment epithelium alterations, and residual peripapillary and extrafoveal subretinal fibrosis in each eye (arrows). Late fluorescein angiograms demonstrate central blockage corresponding to areas of subretinal fibrosis and faint staining of the borders of the fibrosis. Vision was 20/400 in each eye.

pool.q: A 5-year-old male patient presents with a complaint of light sensitivity that his parents say has been present since he was an infant. The family reports intermittent hematuria, as well. On examination, the patient has a small rim of rudimentary iris tissue present bilaterally, and foveal hypoplasia OU. What is the most important next step in diagnosis and management?
pool.rationale: This patient's presentation is concerning for aniridia and Wilms tumor. An association between sporadic aniridia and Wilms tumor has been associated with 11p13 chromosomal deletions and mutations in the PAX6 gene (in the same location). An autosomal dominant pattern of heredity is also associated with aniridia, but not Wilms tumor. Foveal hypoplasia can be seen in association with aniridia, but a fluorescein angiogram would not be the most likely next step in diagnosis and management. Because of the possibility of Wilms tumor, particularly with a history of hematuria, this patient must get imaging of the kidneys, initially with ultrasonography and often magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) after the ultrasonography is done. An x-ray for renal calculi would not show the Wilms tumor unless calcification were present (it is not normally associated with this tumor). Genetic counseling may be indicated in some cases of aniridia, but if the patient has a Wilms tumor, then the patient likely has a sporadic mutation.

pool.q: What lacrimal gland tumor is most likely associated with bone remodeling?
pool.rationale:
Pleomorphic adenoma (or benign mixed tumor) of the lacrimal gland is pseudoencapsulated and slowly grows by expansion, thus indenting the bone of the lacrimal fossa, producing focal excavation of the bone.
Adenoid cystic carcinoma is malignant, aggressive, and rapidly growing, thus causing bone erosion.
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma tends to be diffuse and cause proptosis.
Fibrous histiocytoma most commonly presents in the upper nasal orbit and does not tend to cause bone remodeling.

pool.q: In hemolytic glaucoma, what characteristic material accumulates in the trabecular meshwork?
pool.rationale: Hemolytic glaucoma is characterized by the accumulation of hemosiderin-­laden macrophages in the trabecular meshwork. Rigid hemolyzed erythrocytes are seen following intraocular hemorrhage in ghost cell glaucoma. Pigmented epithelioid melanocytes can invade the trabecular meshwork in the setting of uveal melanomas. In phacolytic glaucoma, eosinophilic ­protein-­laden macrophages are seen within the trabecular meshwork.

pool.q: Histopathologic examination of an excised orbital tumor reveals keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, keratin debris, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles. What lesion was excised?
pool.rationale: Dermoid cysts (figures) are most commonly found near the fronto-zygomatic or naso-frontal sutures. Dermoid cysts are choristomas (normal tissue in an abnormal location) and are similar to epidermoid cysts in that both are cystic structures lined by stratified squamous epithelium. However, by definition, dermoid cysts contain dermal elements such as sebaceous glands, hair follicles, and sweat glands. The cyst cavity fills with keratin debris. Dermoid cysts of the orbit are congenital, but they may not become symptomatic until adult life. They may cause proptosis with bony remodeling of the orbit and can erode into the cranial cavity. Trauma to the orbit can cause rupture with a foreign-body granulomatous inflammatory response.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 35-year-old patient with cognitive impairment, adenoma sebaceum, and sharply delineated hypopigmented lesions on the skin, has the retinal lesion depicted in the image. On optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging, in what layer is the lesion present?
pool.rationale:
This is a retinal astrocytic hamartoma that is confined to the nerve fiber layer. A retinal astrocytic hamartoma is a benign retinal tumor composed of glial cells, predominantly astrocytes. It is believed to be congenital in most cases, but it can become clinically apparent sometime after birth. Retinal astrocytoma may present as 1 or multiple lesions occurring unilaterally or bilaterally. In children, phakomas are relatively flat, with a smooth surface, indistinct margins, and a gray-white color that makes them difficult to detect. A second type of phakoma, more often found in adults, occurs adjacent to or on the optic nerve, with calcified surface yielding a “mulberry” appearance. Retinal astrocytic hamartomas are frequently associated with tuberous sclerosis complex, a syndrome that includes various combinations of low-grade intracranial astrocytoma, cutaneous angiofibromas, cutaneous depigmented macules, cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipoma, and other hamartomas. The exact prevalence of retinal astrocytic hamartoma in tuberous sclerosis is not known.
Approximately one-third to one-half of patients with tuberous sclerosis have retinal or optic nerve hamartoma, and in half of these, the hamartomas occur bilaterally. The tumor can be seen in patients with neurofibromatosis as well. Clinically, the lesion can masquerade as a small retinoblastoma, but handheld OCT imaging can be used to demonstrate that the tumor is confined to the nerve fiber layer.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Conjunctival nevi are most commonly found in what anatomic location?
pool.rationale: Conjunctival melanocytic nevi most commonly appear on the perilimbal interpalpebral bulbar conjunctiva in childhood. Nevi can also occur in the caruncle. Nevi occur only rarely in the palpebral and forniceal conjunctiva.

pool.q: Pathologic examination of an eye reveals a loss of the inner retina (nerve fiber layer, ganglion cells, inner plexiform layer, and inner two-thirds of the inner nuclear layer) and preservation of the outer one-third of the inner nuclear layer and intact outer plexiform, outer nuclear, and photoreceptor layers. What diagnosis can you make from these pathologic findings?
pool.rationale: The retinal blood vessels supply the nerve fiber layer, ganglion cell layer, inner plexiform layer, and the inner two-thirds of the inner nuclear layer. Loss of this vascular supply leads to ischemic necrosis and eventual atrophy of these retinal layers as shown. In contrast, the outer retina (outer one-third of the inner nuclear layer, outer plexiform layer, outer nuclear layer, and photoreceptors) is supplied by the choroidal circulation. Choroidal ischemia would cause loss of these outer retinal layers.

pool.q: How should tissue or fluid be submitted for flow cytometry?
pool.rationale: Flow cytometry is used to identify cell surface markers on cells moving single file in a fluid stream. In ophthalmology, it is most often used to evaluate lymphoid proliferations. Tissue must be sent fresh (without fixative and unfrozen) in a timely manner to prevent cell loss. Fluorochrome-labeled antibodies bound to specific cell surface receptors are sorted by a photodetector. The information gathered is an adjunct to morphologic and immunohistochemistry evaluation performed on additional formalin-fixed tissue. It is performed on vitreous, aqueous, or adnexal tissue, not on solid tumors.

pool.q: By what mechanism does von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) syndrome cause angiogenesis?

options.b: increased vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) transcription

pool.rationale:
Von Hippel–Lindau syndrome leads to angiogenesis, owing to increased VEGF transcription. Retinal capillary hemangioblastomas are a common manifestation of the syndrome (more than 60% of VHL syndrome patients have them). This is the result of mutation of the VHL gene on chromosome 3 that leads to overproduction of VEGF and other hypoxia-inducible factors. Less commonly, cerebellar and/or spinal hemangioblastomas can develop.
Reduced Wnt signaling, increased Rb protein, and VHL polymerization are not mechanisms that lead to angiogenesis in von Hippel–Lindau syndrome.

pool.q: A pathologic specimen of a corneal button is shown below, with arrows indicating subepithelial bullae. What is the most likely cause of the corneal pathology in this case?
pool.rationale:
The corneal button shows subepithelial bullae, stromal edema, and the absence of guttae or Descemet thickening. This is most likely bullous keratopathy secondary to intraocular surgery, such as phacoemulsification of a dense cataract.
Fuchs dystrophy would be expected to show guttae, or focal excrescences in Descemet membrane. Descemet is also typically irregular and thickened.
Keratoconus would result in apical thinning and steepening, and hydrops would show a rupture in Descemet membrane.
Thiel-Behnke corneal dystrophy shows subepithelial honeycomb opacities at the level of Bowman layer that are observed histologically as replacement of Bowman layer with a fibrous pannus in a sawtooth pattern.

pool.q: In keratoconus without hydrops, what layer of the cornea demonstrates focal discontinuities?
pool.rationale: Keratoconus is characterized by inferior or inferotemporal corneal stromal ectasia. Histologic findings in keratoconus include central stromal thinning and focal discontinuities in Bowman layer. The base of the cone may demonstrate a Fleischer ring, which is iron deposited in the basal epithelial cells and may be demonstrated with iron stains such as Prussian blue. In patients with a history of corneal hydrops, a break in Descemet membrane may be observed.

pool.q: In what gene have mutations been found to correlate to nevi of Ota, blue nevi, and uveal melanoma?
pool.rationale:
GNAQ

Mutations in the GNAQ and GNA11 genes have been found in 50%–85% of blue nevi and uveal melanomas and in a smaller percentage of nevi of Ota. They are considered founding mutations in the development of uveal melanoma. PAX6 mutations are associated with congenital eye malformations, including aniridia (WAGR syndrome = Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary malformations, and mental retardation); congenital cataract; ectopia pupillae; Peters anomaly; morning glory disc anomaly; optic nerve hypoplasia; and colobomas of the optic nerve, retina, and choroid. BAP1 gene mutations have been identified in about 80% of uveal melanomas with a poor prognosis (class 2 tumors). Almost half of the tumors from patients with cutaneous melanoma have mutations in the BRAF gene. Mutations in the BRAF gene are only found in uveal melanoma in rare cases.

pool.q: The funduscopic examination of a single patient's left (A) and right (B) eyes is shown in the figure. What is the most likely systemic diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The figure shows a diffuse choroidal hemangioma affecting the left eye. The unaffected right eye also is shown. Diffuse choroidal hemangiomas typically occur in the setting of Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalofacial angiomatosis).
Retinal capillary hemangioblastomas typically occur in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Retinal arteriovenous malformations typically occur in Wyburn-Mason syndrome. Retinal capillary hemangiomas may occur in neurofibromatosis type 1.

pool.q: A 75-year-old man is referred to an ophthalmologist for evaluation of an eyelid lesion (Figure 1). On examination, there is a flat, pale yellow lesion that is firm to palpation. Histology of the lesion is shown in Figure 2. What is the diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The histology shown represents the morpheaform variant of basal cell carcinoma (BCC). BCC appears clinically as a slow growing, elevated lesion with ulceration and pearly raised edges. The morpheaform or sclerosing growth pattern appears as a flat, pale yellow, indurated plaque. This variant is often infiltrative and difficult to stage. Other variants of BCC include nodular and multicentric. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignant eyelid lesion. The main risk factor is sunlight exposure. Lesions are just about as common in the medial canthus (48.3%) as in the lower lid (47.5%). Lesions affecting the medial canthus are more likely to be deeply invasive and involve the orbit. BCC originates from the stratum basale, or stratum germinativum and the outer root sheath of the hair follicles. Histology demonstrated islands of basaloid cells connected to overlying dermis with peripheral palisading. A clear space may surround the islands of tumor cells as a result of artifact in processing. The malignant morpheaform variant shows thin cords and strands of cells infiltrating a fibrotic stroma.
Of patients with BCC, 0.7% have nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome, also known as Gorlin-Goltz syndrome. This autosomal dominant syndrome results in multiple BCCs in young patients, odontogenic jaw cysts, skeletal abnormalities, palmar and plantar pits, neurologic abnormalities, and endocrine disorders. Treatment of choice is complete excision with surgical margin control. This can be achieved with frozen sections or Mohs surgery. Morbidity with BCC is usually secondary to local invasion, as metastasis is extremely rare.

pool.q: In this patient who has granular corneal dystrophy type 1 (GCD1), what type of stain is shown in Figure 1, with hyaline deposits staining red and stromal collagen staining blue?
pool.rationale:
Special stains are used to determine the composition of the deposits in corneal stromal dystrophies. Masson trichrome is used to identify deposits in granular dystrophy in which collagen stains blue and hyaline material stains red.
Alcian blue is used to identify mucopolysaccharide deposition in macular dystrophy.
Congo red stains amyloid orange by standard light microscopy in lattice dystrophy; on examination with polarized light, the amyloid exhibits birefringence with dichroism (orange and apple green).
Periodic acid-Schiff stains glycogen and proteoglycans magenta.

pool.q: What clinical feature typically leads to phthisis bulbi?
pool.rationale: Phthisical globes demonstrate shrinkage, atrophy, and disorganization (SAD eyes). Loss of adequate IOP leads to shrinkage of the eye. A formerly hypertensive eye will often demonstrate normal or low IOP as it becomes phthisical. Phthisical eyes might demonstrate vitreous hemorrhage or hemorrhage in other ocular structures. Intraocular ossification occurs late; it is a typical histologic finding in phthisis bulbi.

pool.q: What pathologic change distinguishes squamous cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva from conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasm (CIN)?
pool.rationale:
Conjunctival and corneal intraepithelial neoplasms are uncommon tumors. The most important assessment to be made histologically in ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN) is whether the neoplasia is contained by the basement membrane, as in conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia (partial-thickness dysplasia of the epithelium), or carcinoma in situ (full-thickness dysplasia of the epithelium), or whether neoplastic cells have invaded the stroma (squamous cell carcinoma).
Altered maturation of cells (dysplasia), nuclear hyperchromatism and pleomorphism, and dyskeratosis are common in both CIN and squamous cell carcinoma.

pool.q: What is the most common intraocular malignant neoplasm?
pool.rationale: Choroidal metastasis is the most common intraocular malignant neoplasm overall. Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignant neoplasm. Primary ocular lymphoma is not the most common intraocular malignant neoplasm. Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignant neoplasm in children, but not the most common intraocular malignant neoplasm overall.

pool.q: Penetrating keratoplasty is performed on a patient with suspected granular dystrophy. What histochemical stain can aid in confirming this dystrophy?
pool.rationale: Masson-­trichrome highlights deposits of hyaline material that characterize granular corneal dystrophy. Congo red stains amyloid deposits in lattice and ­granular-­lattice dystrophies. Alcian blue stains nonsulfated glycosaminoglycan deposits in macular dystrophy.

pool.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with a pigmented lesion of his left eye (see figure). It has been present since birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: A congenital nevocellular nevi is a sharply demarcated, darkly pigmented lesion of the skin that can occur anywhere on the body. Large lesions greater than 20 cm have an increased rate of malignant transformation. A nevus of Ota is a diffusely pigmented dermal lesion that frequently involves the sclera. A nevus flammeus is a congenital vascular anomaly that presents as a red skin lesion that darkens over time. A blue nevus is a small, dark blue-grey dome-shaped dermal lesion of 10 mm or less in size.

pool.q: The corneal deposits in granular dystrophy (figure) are composed of what material?
pool.rationale: Granular corneal stromal dystrophy is an autosomal dominant condition with irregular, well-circumscribed deposits of hyaline material in the corneal stroma (figure). The opacities are initially seen in the central cornea and have intervening clear spaces. The hyaline material stains bright red with Masson trichrome stain as shown and is composed of electron-dense material with rod-shaped bodies in an amorphous matrix. The noncollagenous protein may derive from the corneal epithelium or keratocytes. A mutation in the TGFBI gene on chromosome 5q31 is responsible for the formation of keratoepithelin. Three clinical forms of granular dystrophy are defined, with similar ultrastructural features and variations in the rate of progression, appearance, and depth of the deposits. Avellino corneal dystrophy is a variant of granular dystrophy and has been traced to families in Avellino, Italy. These patients have granular dystrophy but also show lattice stromal dystrophic changes. Different mutations in the TGFB1 (formerly BIGH3) gene are thought to cause granular, Avellino, lattice, and Reis-Bücklers dystrophies. Early symptoms are recurrent erosions. At later stages, superficial keratectomy, photokeratectomy, or corneal transplantation may be indicated.

pool.q: What is the key pathology finding that distinguishes a teratoid medulloepithelioma from a non-teratoid medulloepithelioma?
pool.rationale:
Heteroplastic tissue is defined as the presence of tissue arising from 2 or more different embryonic germ layers. Teratoid medulloepitheliomas contain tissue that is not of ectodermal origin, such as cartilage or skeletal muscle.
Retina, vitreous, and ciliary body epithelium are all derived from ectoderm.

pool.q: A 1-year-old child presents with a bright red lesion of the upper eyelid that has existed since birth but has recently been enlarging in size. There is mild, symmetric astigmatism in both eyes. The mother insists on treatment to remove the entire lesion. What is the best treatment option?
pool.rationale:
Capillary hemangiomas are common eyelid lesions in children. These may appear at or shortly after birth and clinically appear as bright red lesions that grow rapidly over weeks to months. These lesions are nonencapsulated and usually involute spontaneously. Histologic appearance depends on the stage. Early lesions show sheets of benign endothelial cells surrounding capillary channels. Involuting lesions display increased fibrosis and hyalinization of capillary walls. Although lesions eventually involute and regress, they can pose a risk for amblyopia.
β-blockers are often used as first-line treatment of capillary hemangiomas, usually with significant reduction in size. Excision of these lesions should be performed with care because it can lead to significant blood loss from the large feeder vessels that are present within the hemangiomas. Historically, treatment for vision-threatening or cosmetically unacceptable lesions has included injection of steroids. This presentation is inconsistent with amblyopia, because the refractive correction is symmetric. Injection of steroids has the potential complication of central retinal artery occlusion and should be reserved for nonresponsive, vision-threatening lesions.

pool.q: A patient presents with an eyelid mass. What is the most frequent indication for a frozen section?

options.a: to surgically control the margins of a neoplasm
options.b: to make a diagnosis more expediently
options.d: to interpret a melanocytic cutaneous lesion

pool.rationale: Frozen sections are appropriate to ensure complete resection of the neoplasm. Frozen sections are generally not recommended on melanocytic lesions because of the potential for artifact. A formal diagnosis should be made on permanent sections. Frozen sections should not be used as means to expedite a diagnosis.

pool.q: From highest to lowest, what is the order of mortality rates for iris, ciliary body and choroidal melanomas?

options.a: choroidal melanoma > ciliary body melanoma > iris melanoma
options.b: ciliary body melanoma > choroidal melanoma > iris melanoma
options.c: choroidal melanoma > iris melanoma > ciliary body melanoma
options.d: iris melanoma > ciliary body melanoma > choroidal melanoma

pool.rationale: Uveal melanomas can arise in the anterior (iris) or the posterior (ciliary body or choroid) uveal tract. Iris melanomas have the best prognosis, whereas posterior melanomas have a high mortality rate. Melanomas of the ciliary body have the least favorable prognosis, possibly because they may be more frequently diagnosed at a later stage.

pool.q: What syndrome may include the lesion shown in the figures?
pool.rationale:
The photo shows an epibulbar dermoid. Dermoids are firm, dome-shaped, white-yellow choristomas typically at or straddling the limbus, most commonly in the inferotemporal quadrant. Dermoids may occur in isolation or, particularly when bilateral, as a manifestation of a developmental syndrome such as linear nevus sebaceous syndrome or Goldenhar syndrome. Goldenhar syndrome is characterized by upper eyelid coloboma, preauricular skin tags, and vertebral anomalies in addition to epibulbar dermoid.

pool.q: What is the most common histopathological finding in temporal arteritis?

pool.q: What is the most common cause of infectious retinitis?

pool.q: A patient who recently relocated from another city presents to establish care for an "eye tumor" OD. Records from his previous ophthalmologist are presently unavailable, and he is unsure of the exact diagnosis, but he tells the new ophthalmologist that the lesion has been stable for years. On examination, a jet-black elevated mass originating from the prelaminar nerve extending into the peripapillary region is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.d: congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE)

pool.rationale:
Melanocytomas, also known as magnocellular nevi, are uncommon melanocytic uveal tumors that are deeply pigmented, and often peripapillary in location. These lesions are typically dark brown or even jet black and can be mistaken for melanomas; however, they rarely transform into melanoma. Documented growth should prompt work-up for possible melanoma. Melanocytomas may be elevated and often have feathery margins due to extension into the nerve fiber layer, and as such can cause a relative afferent pupillary defect and visual field defects.
Histologically, large polyhedral cells that are densely packed with melanin and have small nucleoli are seen. Often, there is so much pigment that it is necessary to bleach the section in order to make a diagnosis. Choroidal nevi and congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) are other pigmented uveal lesions that would not be expected to change over time; however, in this case the peripapillary location is more suggestive of a melanocytoma. Choroidal melanoma would not be expected to maintain stability over time.

pool.q: What is the normal timeframe after a corneal abrasion for the epithelial anchoring fibrils to reform?
pool.rationale: Within an hour of a corneal abrasion, the parabasilar epithelial cells begin to migrate across the denuded area until they touch other migrating cells; then contact inhibition stops further migration. Simultaneously, the surrounding basal cells undergo mitosis to supply additional cells to cover the defect. Although a large corneal abrasion is usually covered by migrating epithelial cells within 24 to 48 hours, complete healing, which includes restoration of the full thickness of epithelium (5-7 layers) and re-formation of the anchoring fibrils, takes 4 to 6 weeks.

pool.q: What stain is used to identify the elastosis of degenerated collagen in pingueculae and pterygia?

Histologic examination of stromal collagen in pingueculae and pterygia shows fragmentation and basophilic degeneration, referred to as elastotic degeneration or solar elastosis. Verhoeff-van Gieson stains the elastin, even after the tissue has been treated with elastase for digestion of true elastin.

This can be useful for conjunctival amyloid deposits or lattice corneal dystrophy. pool.q: A 55-year-old white man presents without symptoms for evaluation. His ocular history is unremarkable. His slit-lamp examination is abnormal, as shown. What is his most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: The figure shows tarsal pigment in a white patient. This presentation is most consistent with primary acquired melanosis. pool.q: Corneal limbal dermoids are classified as what type of lesion?
pool.rationale: Corneal limbal dermoids (figures) are choristomas, which are tumors composed of mature normal tissue that is present at an abnormal location. They are present at birth with little postnatal growth. They consist of various amounts of normal mature tissue (keratinized dermal epithelium, dermal collagen, adipose tissue, dermal appendages such as hair follicles or sebaceous or acinar sweat glands, peripheral nerves) in an abnormal location on the corneal surface, often straddling the limbus. Corneal dermoids are solid tumors, in contrast to orbital dermoid cysts. There is a frequent association with Goldenhar syndrome (preauricular appendages or aural fistulae, maxillary or mandibular hypoplasia, vertebral anomalies, eyelid cleft abnormalities, and Duane syndrome). Excision is often indicated because of irritation, cosmesis, and interference with vision. Tissue should be available for patch grafting in case the dissection is too deep, but usually superficial removal suffices.

pool.q: What optic nerve cells produce and maintain the myelin sheath?

Oligodendrocytes produce and maintain the myelin sheath of the optic nerve; astrocytes are involved with support and nutrition; and microglial cells (central nervous system [CNS] histiocytes) have a phagocytic function. The axons of retinal ganglion cells are contained within the optic nerve.

pool.q: A child with a history of yellow-red skin lesions presents with unilateral recurrent hyphema. A few iris nodules are noted. What histologic findings would be expected on skin or iris biopsy?

options.a: large histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and Touton giant cells

Bilateral diffuse uveal melanocytic proliferation is characterized by infiltration of the uveal tract by benign nevoid or spindle-shaped cells. pool.q: Retinal astrocytic hamartomas are most associated with what systemic condition?
pool.rationale:
Tuberous sclerosis complex (Bourneville-Pringle disease) is an autosomal dominant condition that may be associated with astrocytic hamartomas in the retina, optic disc, and brain. The figures show selected findings. The retinal lesions may be relatively flat, gray-white lesions with indistinct margins, or they may be sharply demarcated and elevated, containing multiple, reflective, calcific spherules. The retinal tumors are seen in approximately 40% of patients. Growth is slow, and vision is usually not affected. They may rarely cause exudative changes requiring photocoagulation. These are not pathognomonic of tuberous sclerosis. Similar hamartomas are seen occasionally in neurofibromatosis and in normal patients. Retinal lesions are more common in patients with the TSC2 mutation. These 2 proteins form a heterodimer that normally inhibits cell proliferation. The mechanisms of these gene defects that lead to the clinical findings in tuberous sclerosis are not known, but more than 400 mutations have been described.
The classic triad (Vogt triad) in tuberous sclerosis is facial sebaceous adenomas (angiofibromas), mental deficiency, and seizures. Other dermatologic features include periungual fibromas, cafe-au-lait spots, shagreen patches, and the pathognomonic "ash-leaf" spot. Many of the tumors in tuberous sclerosis are hamartomas. Visceral tumors including cardiac rhabdomyomas, renal cysts, and angiomyolipomas may occur. Brain tumors are cortical tubers and subependymal nodules, containing glial and neuronal elements that often calcify.

pool.q: What primary cellular element is observed histologically in the preretinal membranes found in proliferative vitreoretinopathy?

Unless there is rupture of Bruch membrane, choroidal melanocytes do not have access to the subretinal space or vitreous cavity and therefore are not typically observed in PVR membranes.

pool.q: What effect on survival did the Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study demonstrate for pre-enucleation external beam radiation in patients with large melanomas?
pool.rationale:
The Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study compared standard enucleation against enucleation with presurgical radiation therapy and showed that there is no evidence that pre-enucleation external-beam radiotherapy on patients with large choroidal melanomas improves 5-year mortality rates. However, local recurrence in the orbit was more frequent after enucleation alone. While details of the study are not included in the BCSC, here is a brief summary of the details. There were 1003 patients enrolled in the study, and 5-year outcomes were known for nearly 80% of the study population. The 5-year survival rates were 57% for enucleation alone, and 62% for pre-enucleation radiation. No significant difference was found in survival between the 2 groups from all causes of metastatic melanoma. In the enucleation-alone group, 26% died from confirmed metastatic melanoma, compared to 28% in the preenucleation radiation group.
Other issues to be considered with the use of pre-enucleation external beam radiation include the added cost of radiation, the risk of induced secondary tumors in the radiation field, secondary ptosis, patient inconvenience, and the delay in enucleation with the risk of local extension or recurrence. In contrast, radioactive plaque application to the sclera overlying a choroidal melanoma is probably the most common form of treatment (figure). Local tumor control rates are as high as 90%, with late complications of radiation optic neuropathy and maculopathy.

pool.q: A 49-year-old woman presents with right eye pain. The slit-lamp examination reveals ciliary flush, anterior chamber cell, mutton-fat keratic precipitates, and posterior synechiae. The patient states that she has had similar episodes of this pain in the past. Further examination reveals small tan nodules in the lower conjunctival fornices. What would a conjunctival biopsy be expected to reveal?

options.d: linear deposition of immunoglobulins and complement C3 on the conjunctival basement membrane

pool.rationale:
This patient has recurrent granulomatous uveitis secondary to sarcoidosis. The small tan nodules in the conjunctival fornices are indicative of granulomatous conjunctivitis. Noncaseating granulomas would be expected on conjunctival biopsy. These are round to oval aggregates of epithelioid histocytes with or without multinucleated giant cells. These pathologic findings alone are not pathognomonic for sarcoidosis but must be correlated with clinical findings after infectious causes are ruled out.
Linear deposition of immunoglobulins and complement (C3) on the basement membrane would be found in mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP) and would not be associated with granulomatous uveitis.
Gram-positive cocci in pairs would be indicative of infection with Streptococcus spp. These infections would not be associated with granulomatous uveitis.
Elastotic degeneration is the pathologic finding in pinguecula and pterygium.

pool.q: What stain can be useful to obtain after biopsying the eyelid of an individual with a chronic, unilateral papillary conjunctivitis?

On biopsy, it is important to pay attention to histopathologic characteristics, including presence of anaplastic cells, multiple mitoses, and lipid. pool.q: Leukemic retinopathy can cause hemorrhages in what levels of the retina?

options.b: It does not cause retinal hemorrhages.

pool.rationale:
Posterior segment findings in leukemia include retinal hemorrhages, white-centered hemorrhages (pseudo-Roth spots), cotton-wool spots, subhyaloid hemorrhage, vitreous hemorrhage, and subretinal or choroidal hemorrhage. Retinal vascular occlusions are common. Retinal hemorrhages are caused by vascular occlusions and concomitant anemia and thrombocytopenia. Perivascular infiltration of leukemic cells can give vessels a sheathed appearance or produce yellow-gray nodules in the retina or subretinal space.
Leukemia also frequently involves the uvea. Choroidal infiltrates can be difficult to see on examination, but can be detected as diffuse choroidal thickening on ultrasonography. The iris may be thickened by leukemic cells, and these cells can invade the anterior chamber, forming a pseudohypopyon and secondary glaucoma.
Leukemic infiltration of the optic nerve may present with disc edema and severe vision loss. This should be treated urgently with systemic and intrathecal chemotherapy plus radiation to preserve vision.
All the eye findings of leukemia can be caused by 1 or more of the following: increased viscosity from increased numbers of leukemic cells, hemorrhage due to decreased platelets and alteration in the clotting cascade, and infiltration of tissues by leukemic cells.

pool.q: What ancillary test is most useful in the initial evaluation of choroidal melanoma?

options.b: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the orbit

pool.rationale:
Ultrasonography is considered the most useful ancillary tool in evaluating choroidal melanomas. A- and B-scan ultrasonography are used to measure choroidal melanoma size, to evaluate internal tumor reflectivity, and to evaluate for the presence of extrascleral extension. Standardized A-scan typically demonstrates high initial reflectivity followed by low-amplitude internal reflections (low internal reflectivity). B-scan can inform the examiner about the thickness, basal diameter, and general shape of the mass.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is not a widely used modality in assessing melanocytic intraocular tumors, but it has utility in assessing eyes with opaque media and can provide information regarding possible extrascleral extension. OCT may be better than ultrasonography in trending choroidal lesions <1 mm in thickness and can also provide diagnostic information regarding the architecture of the neurosensory retina and retinal pigment epithelium. Fluorescein angiography is used to detect the presence of an independent tumor circulation, a supportive but not definitively diagnostic finding in choroidal melanoma. Indocyanine green angiography may also identify local alterations in choroidal blood flow.

pool.q: If a conjunctival biopsy is being performed for suspicion of ocular cicatricial pemphigoid (OCP), then half of the specimen should be submitted in formalin for routine histology and the other half should be submitted in what medium for immunofluorescence studies?

OCP is a form of autoimmune cicatrizing conjunctivitis of autoimmune etiology. Typically, it involves not only the conjunctiva but also other mucous membranes. When this diagnosis is suspected clinically, conjunctival biopsy is performed to establish the diagnosis. pool.q: What is a common histopathologic finding in aphakic/pseudophakic bullous keratopathy?

options.b: fibrous growth in the anterior chamber
options.d: vascular changes in the epithelial layer

Intraocular surgery, most often cataract surgery, results in loss of endothelial cells. The loss of endothelial cells may lead to bullous keratopathy, characterized by Descemet folds, stromal edema, epithelial edema, and microcystic epithelial separations or bullae. Other forms of intraocular surgery, including multiple and/or complicated glaucoma procedures, may lead to similar findings.
Epithelialization of the endothelial cells may be present in posterior polymorphous dystrophy, iridocorneal endothelial syndrome, and epithelial ingrowth.

pool.q: What pathologic findings characterize the inflammation in phacoantigenic uveitis (also known as phacoanaphylactic endophthalmitis or lens-induced granulomatous endophthalmitiis)?

Phacoantigenic uveitis is usually associated with penetrating ocular injuries with rupture of the lens capsule. The exposed lens material provokes a granulomatous inflammation. The zonal granuloma demonstrates multinucleated giant cells and neutrophils adjacent to the lens material, with an intermediate mantle of lymphocytes and histiocytes and surrounding fibrous connective tissue with chronic inflammation.

pool.q: Fuchs dystrophy can be identified based on the pathologic examination of thickening of what layer?

pool.q: What clinical finding is a risk factor for malignant transformation of a choroidal nevus?
pool.rationale:
Choroidal nevi rarely transform into malignant melanoma. By age 80, a patient's risk of malignant transformation of an existing choroidal nevus is about 0.8%.
The most important risk factor for malignant transformation is nevus thickness. Virtually all choroidal melanocytic tumors thinner than 1 mm are nevi, and virtually all choroidal melanocytic lesions thicker than 3 mm are melanomas. Lesions between 1 mm and 2 mm in thickness can be difficult to classify, and close observation is often recommended. Lesions between 2 mm and 3 mm in thickness may be managed based on clinical risk factors with observation or immediate treatment.
Other predictive risk factors for malignant transformation include subretinal fluid, subjective clinical symptoms (metamorphopsia, photopsia, visual field loss), presence of overlying orange pigment, lack of overlying drusen, juxtapapillary location, basal dimension 7 mm or greater, and low to medium internal reflectivity on A-scan echography.

pool.q: Histologically, what are the most common type of cells in a choroidal melanoma?

Less commonly, balloon cells similar to those seen in choroidal nevi may be present. Spindle-cell melanoma consists primarily of spindle-B melanoma cells. It may also contain spindle-A cells; however, a tumor consisting entirely of spindle-A cells is considered a nevus. Monocytes and Touton giant cells are inflammatory cells.

pool.q: What anterior segment finding(s) is (are) characteristic of Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome?
