pool.q: What disorder typically results in Touton giant cells in histologic specimens?
pool.rationale: The Touton giant cell can be distinguished by the presence of several nuclei in a distinct pattern: a ring of nuclei surrounds a central homogeneous, eosinophilic cytoplasm; and foamy cytoplasm surrounds the nuclei. Touton giant cells are seen in lesions with high lipid content, such as fat necrosis, xanthomas, and xanthogranulomas. Both bacterial keratitis and Acanthamoeba keratitis are characterized histologically by a dense infiltrate of neutrophils with variable tissue necrosis. Follicular cell lymphoma is characterized histologically by closely packed follicles that contain atypical lymphoid cells.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 35-year-old patient develops hypotony after blunt ocular trauma. What pathologic abnormality is demonstrated in this ultrasound biomicroscopy image?

options.a: separation of the ciliary body from the scleral spur
options.c: disinsertion of the iris root from ciliary body
options.d: tear between the circular and longitudinal fibers of ciliary body

pool.rationale: Prolonged hypotony after blunt ocular trauma may be due to a cyclodialysis cleft, as found in this patient. In this condition, the ciliary body separates from the scleral spur, providing direct access of aqueous to the suprachoroidal space. Gonioscopy can be difficult to perform and interpret in these patients due to a shallow anterior chamber and soft eye (from hypotony). Anterior segment OCT and ultrasound biomicroscopy can be helpful in these cases to evaluate for the presence and extent of a cyclodialysis cleft. Disinsertion of the iris root results in iridodialysis. A tear between the circular and longitudinal fibers of the ciliary body is found in angle recession, seen as a widened ciliary body band on gonioscopy. A tear of the trabecular meshwork may be seen as a small trabecular cleft on gonioscopy. None of these conditions except a cyclodialysis cleft can cause hypotony.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In what gene are polymorphisms associated with pseudoexfoliation syndrome?
pool.rationale:
LOXL1

Polymorphisms in the lysyl oxidase-like 1 gene (LOXL1) are associated with pseudoexfoliation syndrome. Lysyl oxidase is a pivotal enzyme in extracellular matrix formation, catalyzing covalent crosslinking of collagen and elastin. FOXC1 and PITX2 mutations are associated with Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome. PAX6 mutations are associated with developmental abnormalities, such as aniridia and Peters anomaly.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: By what mechanism does orbital extension of choroidal melanomas most often occur?
pool.rationale: Choroidal melanomas can extend through scleral emissary canals into the orbit. Superficial invasion of the sclera is often seen, but extension through intact sclera into the orbit is extremely rare. Retinoblastoma can invade the lamina cribrosa, extending into the optic nerve and brain; however, uveal melanoma does not typically invade the optic nerve or brain. The irradiation (eg, brachytherapy) used to treat choroidal melanomas does not usually lead to scleromalacia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Choroidal metastasis from what primary malignancy is most common in women?
pool.rationale: Choroidal metastasis most commonly arises from the breast in women and second most-commonly from the lung. The lung is the most common site of primary malignancy in men.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 52-year-old man presents with the subconjunctival finding shown in the figure. What pathology finding would be consistent with a fibrous histiocytoma?

options.a: activated spindled fibroblasts loosely arranged in short fascicles with a prominent capillary network
options.b: proliferation of spindle fibroblasts, wounded histiocytes, and occasional multinucleated giant cells
options.c: palisading arrangement of epithelioid histiocytes around a central core of necrotic collagen
options.d: basophilic calcific deposits in the sclera anterior to the lateral rectus muscle

pool.rationale: Basophilic calcific deposits in the sclera anterior to the lateral rectus muscle are consistent with senile calcific plaque. Activated spindled fibroblasts loosely arranged in short fascicles with a prominent capillary network are consistent with scleral nodular fasciitis. A palisading arrangement of epithelioid histiocytes around a central core of necrotic collagen is consistent with episcleritis. Finally, proliferation of spindle fibroblasts, wounded histiocytes, and occasional multinucleated giant cells is consistent with fibrous histiocytoma or fibroxanthoma. (See figure).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What histologic change corresponds to commotio retinae?

options.a: disruption of myelin in the nerve fiber layer (NFL)
options.b: presence of subretinal fluid (localized neurosensory detachment)
options.c: ischemia of the nerve fiber layer
options.d: disruption in the architecture of the inner and outer segments of the photoreceptors

pool.rationale: The changes resulting from contusion injury to the retina manifest clinically as areas of retinal whitening. For many years, it was believed that this indicated a possible diagnosis of retinal edema or focal ischemia, both of which demonstrate retinal opacification clinically. The advent of optical coherence tomography showed that retinal whitening can also correspond to disruption in the architecture of the retinal photoreceptor inner and outer segments. The presence of subretinal fluid does not significantly change the color of the ocular fundus. Microinfarcts of the nerve fiber layer (NFL), or ­cotton-­wool spots, are located in the superficial retina. Myelin is not typically present in the retinal NFL; ganglion cell axons acquire myelin sheaths posterior to the lamina cribrosa.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What stain best demonstrates the histological stromal deposits in macular corneal dystrophy?
pool.rationale: Macular corneal dystrophy (MCD) is an autosomal recessive condition with bilateral limbus to limbus deposition of mucopolysaccharides within the cornea (first figure). The mucopolysaccharides are positively stained by alcian blue and colloidal iron stains (second figure). Clinically there are focal gray-white stromal opacities, with hazy intervening stroma and early visual loss within the first decade of life. In contrast to the other major stromal dystrophies, the corneal endothelium is often also involved. The glycosaminoglycans accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum of the keratocytes and endothelial cells and extracellularly within the stroma. Three subtypes of MCD have been described based on immunoreactive stains for keratan sulfate.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Histologically, optic nerve head melanocytoma is consistent with what melanocytic tumor?
pool.rationale:
Melanocytomas (magnocellular nevi) are rare tumors composed of characteristic large, polyhedron-shaped nevus cells that have small nuclei and abundant cytoplasm filled with large melanin granules. Magnocellular nevus of the ciliary body or optic nerve head typically appears as a dark brown to black lesion. It is usually located eccentrically over the optic nerve head, and it may be elevated. It often has fibrillar or feathery margins as a result of extension into the nerve fiber layer. Because a melanocytoma rarely transforms into melanoma, it is important to differentiate the two. Melanocytomas can produce an afferent pupillary defect and visual field abnormalities ranging from an enlarged blind spot to extensive nerve fiber layer defects.
Combined hamartoma of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and retina is a rare disorder that occurs most frequently near the optic nerve head margin, though it may also be observed in the peripheral fundus. Typically, the hamartoma appears as a pigmented, slightly elevated lesion with vitreoretinal traction and tortuous retinal vessels. Glial cells within this lesion may contract, producing traction lines seen clinically in the retina. Exudative complications associated with the vascular component of the lesion may be seen. These lesions have been mistaken for melanomas because of their pigmentation, slight elevation, and propensity to change in young individuals.
Hyperplasia of the pigmented ciliary epithelium or the RPE usually develops in response to trauma, inflammation, or other ocular insults.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In Schnabel cavernous optic atrophy, what material can be histopathologically demonstrated in the optically clear spaces within the optic nerve?
pool.rationale:
Schnabel initially described cavernous optic nerve atrophy (figure) in 1892. Extremely high intraocular pressures (IOP) can lead to infarction of the optic nerve, as the vascular supply to the post-laminar nerve from the short posterior ciliary arteries is compromised. Initially, the infarction is manifested by ischemic swelling of the nerve, but this is followed by glial phagocytosis of the necrotic nerve fiber bundles, leaving large, cavernous spaces separated by the pial septae. The cavernous spaces were previously thought to contain vitreous, but are now believed to contain mucopolysaccharides. This unique form of optic nerve atrophy also is seen with vascular disease involving the proximal optic nerve, including atherosclerosis and vasculitis.
Inborn errors of metabolism can lead to ganglioside accumulation in diseases such as Tay-Sachs, not Schnabel cavernous atrophy. Cholesterol and amyloid are not found in this disease process, either.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An 85-year-old white man is referred for a suspicious subretinal process in the right eye. He is asymptomatic. On examination, the vision is 20/30 OU with pseudophakia on slit-lamp examination. His left fundus demonstrates small and medium-sized drusen. His right fundus demonstrates drusen and a temporal subretinal pigmented lesion measuring 10 mm in base and 4.5 mm in thickness. Ultrasonography demonstrates a subretinal lesion with medium or high internal reflectivity. There are no vascular pulsations seen. Fluorescein angiography demonstrates decreased choroidal filling in the area of the lesion. What is the most appropriate management?
pool.rationale:
The diagnosis is peripheral exudative hemorrhagic chorioretinopathy (also termed peripheral or exudative disciform lesion). Most likely this is secondary to a leaking choroidal neovascular membrane outside the macular area. This is most common in the older age group and is often seen in patients with concurrent macular degeneration. Often, these lesions will have associated surrounding subretinal hemorrhage. However, the clinical appearance may simply be a peripheral pigmented choroidal mass. They tend to be acoustically dense (though extremely acoustically hollow may also be seen). The most diagnostic sign is the absence of choroidal spontaneous vascular pulsation within the lesion, which is more indicative of a uveal melanoma.
Fluorescein angiography would reveal early hypofluorescence due to blockage by hemorrhage and late hypofluorescence or hyperfluorescence with retinal pigment epithelial atrophy or hypertrophy.  Observation of this lesion is indicated. In 1 month, it is very likely that the lesion would resolve or regress enough to indicate the diagnosis. On needle biopsy, the cytologic specimen will be mostly red blood cells. One may also see an immediate deflation of the mass when the needle passes into the lesion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is a feature of mild persistent fetal vasculature?
pool.rationale: Persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) is a congenital sporadic condition in infants. It is unilateral in two-thirds of cases. The spectrum of PFV ranges from mild cases with prominent hyaloid vessel remnants, a large Mittendorf dot, and a Bergmeister papilla to severe cases with microphthalmia, ciliary process elongation (classic for PFV), a retrolenticular plaque, a thick, fibrous persistent hyaloid artery, and prominent radial iris vessels. Retinoblastoma may be part of the initial differential diagnosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What tissue response occurs within the lens epithelium in the setting of anoxic or hypoxic injury, such as posterior synechiae or markedly elevated intraocular pressure (IOP)?
pool.rationale: In circumstances that make the lenticular epithelium anoxic or hypoxic, such as posterior synechiae or markedly elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), a metaplastic response may occur, producing fibrous plaques intermixed with basement membrane.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A teenager undergoes evaluation of a unilateral conjunctival mass (part A of the figure below). It is slightly elevated without signs of inflammation or vascularization, and is irregularly pigmented. Biomicroscopy shows multiple small cystic structures within the pigmented mass as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: The description is most compatible with a benign conjunctival nevus, which are common conjunctival lesions. Cystic changes within the lesions are highly suggestive of nevi. Conjunctival nevi may not acquire visible melanin pigment until puberty, or may remain amelanotic. They are usually flat near the limbus, and slightly elevated at other sites (bulbar conjunctiva, caruncle, and eyelid margin). Conjunctival nevi pathologically demonstrate typical nevus cells, with benign nuclei, nesting tendencies, and melanin pigment in approximately 70%. Conjunctival nevi proliferate in the junctional area of the epithelium and then "fall off" into the substantia propria of the conjunctiva. Many conjunctival nevi have associated small epithelium cysts lined by stratified squamous epithelium, often with goblet cells, in the substantia propria (part B of the image shown with the question). These cysts may be seen with the biomicroscope. Inflammation can cause vascular injection, and rapid growth can occur at puberty. Melanomas of the conjunctiva are rare in children. Pyogenic granulomas are granulation tissue at the site of injury, from ruptured chalazia or sutures from pterygium or strabismus surgery. Corneal limbal dermoids are opaque corneal/limbal choristomas with characteristic choristomatous elements including adipose tissue and hair follicles.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What type of cell is shown in this specimen from a choroidal nevus?
pool.rationale:
Choroidal nevi may be composed of 4 types of cells: plump polyhedral nevus cells, slender spindle nevus cells, plump fusiform dendritic nevus cells, and balloon cells. The cells pictured here are spindle cells. 
Melanocytoma is composed of large polyhedral cells. Melanomas can be composed of epithelioid melanoma cells. Choroidal osteomas are composed of compact bone, with intratrabecular spaces that are filled with loose connective tissue that contains large and small blood vessels, vacuolated mesenchymal cells, and scattered mast cells.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The histopathology demonstrated in this photo is most characteristic of what disorder of the uveal tract?
pool.rationale: The histopathology photo is demonstrative of Touton giant cells, which are characteristic of juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG), a benign non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Touton giant cells consist of a ring or horseshoe-shaped arrangement of nuclei containing a central area of eosinophilic cytoplasm, with surrounding foamy cytoplasm around this nuclear arrangement. Behçet disease, sympathetic ophthalmia, and sarcoidosis can all affect the uveal tract but do not demonstrate this unique histopathology.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Xanthelasma most commonly occur in patients with what cholesterol level?

options.d: normal high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and low-density lipoprotein (LDL)

pool.rationale: Xanthelasma are flat, yellowish skin lesions typically found on the upper and lower eyelids, around the inner canthus in middle-aged people. These lesions are frequently seen in patients with elevated serum cholesterol levels (in up to 50% of cases), but they are more common in patients with normal cholesterol levels. They can also be seen in young people with disorders of lipid metabolism. Presence of xanthelasma does not require workup in older patients, but appropriate workup is justified, especially in younger patients. These lesions are composed of lipid-laden or "foamy" histiocytes that aggregate in the superficial dermis around blood vessels. These lesions may be observed. For patients who request removal, options include surgical excision, CO2 or argon laser, or application of trichloroacetic acid (TCA). It is important to inform patients that these lesions may recur. Care must be taken with surgical excision, as removal of significant portions of the anterior lamella may lead to cicatricial ectropion. Laser application can also lead to significant scarring and ectropion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What histopathologic finding is typically seen in congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED)?
pool.rationale:
Histopathological findings in congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) are very similar to those seen in pseudophakic/aphakic bullous keratopathy and include thickened Descemet membrane and focal or diffuse endothelial atrophy. The primary abnormality in CHED is thought to be degeneration of endothelial cells during or after the fifth month of gestation and not the result of surgical trauma as in pseudophakic/aphakic bullous keratopathy.
A multilaminar endothelium may be seen in CHED but is less common. Thinned corneal stroma and atrophic corneal epithelium are not usually associated with CHED.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What component of the vitreous serves as a scaffold for vitreoretinal membrane formation?
pool.rationale: The collagen fibrils of the vitreous can provide a scaffold for glial and fibrovascular tissue from the retina and uveal tract to grow and extend into the vitreous to proliferate as membranes. These membranes usually have a contractile component, which can lead to retinal traction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 13-year-old boy presents with redness of the right eye, constant epiphora, and umbilicated, nodular, waxy lesions on the lid margin. What kind of conjunctivitis does this patient most likely have?
pool.rationale: Molluscum contagiosum, which is caused by a member of the poxvirus family, is characterized by ­dome-­shaped, waxy epidermal nodules with a central umbilication. If present on the eyelid margin, these nodules can cause a secondary follicular conjunctivitis. Histologically, the epithelial nuclei are displaced peripherally by large eosinophilic (pink) viral inclusions known as molluscum or ­Henderson-­Patterson bodies. As the infected cells migrate to the surface, the viral inclusions become more basophilic (blue/dark purple). Bacterial conjunctivitis is associated with a papillary reaction and purulent discharge. In pseudomembranous conjunctivitis, the fibrin network is easily peeled off, leaving the conjunctiva intact; pseudomembranes form on the conjunctiva. Giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC) occurs in primary and secondary forms, all of which are at least partially caused by chronic ocular allergy. Primary forms of GPC include vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis. Secondary GPC is caused by contact lenses, ocular prostheses, or exposed sutures.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: From what material are optic nerve drusen believed to develop?
pool.rationale: Drusen of the optic nerve head are calcific, usually bilateral, deposits embedded within the parenchyma of crowded discs and abnormal vasculature. Evidence suggests that abnormal axonal metabolism leads to mitochondrial calcification and drusen formation. Hard macular drusen are composed of hyaline material.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What anterior corneal dystrophy is associated with corneal tissue that stains positively with Masson Trichrome and Congo red?
pool.rationale: Granular type 2 dystrophy (formerly Avellino dystrophy) has features of both granular type 1 and lattice dystrophies. It stains positively with Masson trichrome as well as Congo red. Granular type 1 dystrophy stains positively with Masson trichrome but not with Congo red. Lattice dystrophy stains positively with Congo red but not Masson trichrome. Macular dystrophy stains positive with Alcian blue but negatively with trichrome and Congo red.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient is a survivor of bilateral retinoblastoma. What is the chance that the patient's children will be affected by retinoblastoma?
pool.rationale:
Retinoblastoma is caused by a mutation in the RB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 13 (13q14). Both copies of the RB1 gene must be mutated in order for a tumor to form.
If a patient has bilateral retinoblastoma, there is an approximately 98% chance that they have a germline mutation. Therefore, the children of a bilateral retinoblastoma survivor have a 50% chance of inheriting one abnormal gene from the affected parent. Of those who inherit the abnormal gene, 90% develop somatic mutations in the remaining normal RB1 allele, leading to multiple tumors in one or both eyes. Thus, the chance that a bilateral retinoblastoma survivor will have a child with retinoblastoma is 45%. (50% chance of inheriting the abnormal RB1 allele and 90% chance of penetrance). About 10% of retinoblastoma patients have a family history of retinoblastoma.
Sporadic cases with no family history make up about 90% of all retinoblastomas. Of these, 60% will have unilateral disease and no germline mutations. The remaining 40% have new germline mutations and will develop multiple tumors. Of note, approximately 15% of the sporadic unilateral patients are carriers of a germline RB1 mutation. Unless there are multiple tumors in the affected eye, these patients are indistinguishable from children without a germline mutation. Genetic counseling for retinoblastoma can be very complex. A survivor of unilateral retinoblastoma has a 7% to 15% chance of having an affected child.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What diagnosis is demonstrated by the histopathology image shown?
pool.rationale:
Phacoantigenic uveitis develops when an amount of lens cortex is retained in an eye following cataract extraction or following traumatic lens capsule disruption. Histopathology (see figure with caption) will show zonal granulomatous inflammation at the site of lenticular trauma. The inflammation can be either granulomatous or nongranulomatous, with corresponding keratic precipitates.
Phacolytic uveitis occurs when a hypermature cataract develops and high-molecular-weight lens proteins leak through the capsular bag into the anterior chamber. Macrophages ingest the lens proteins and become lipid laden, having a refractile appearance. Keratic precipitates in phacolytic uveitis are not typically seen.
The treatment for both types of uveitis is typically surgical: Removal of the lens material will often cause resolution of the uveitis. If a very small amount of cortex is left in the anterior chamber in the case of phacoantigenic uveitis, topical corticosteroids are sometimes employed to manage modest inflammation until the lens material is resorbed by macrophages.
Infectious endophthalmitis is a clinical diagnosis, and an aqueous or vitreous specimen may grow the infectious agent. IOL-associated uveitis such as uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema syndrome is generally related to chafing of intraocular tissue by an intraocular lens.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What clinical feature of conjunctival melanomas is associated with a poor prognosis?
pool.rationale:
Approximately 50%–70% of cases of conjunctival melanoma arise from PAM with atypia; the remainder develop from a nevus or are de novo. Melanomas are usually nodular and can involve any portion of the conjunctiva. The nodule may be pigmented or amelanotic (15%–25% of conjunctival melanomas). Conjunctival melanomas metastasize to regional lymph nodes in 25% of patients, as well as to the lungs, liver, brain, bone, and skin. The overall mortality rate in these cases ranges from 15% to 30%. Clinical features associated with a worse prognosis include:
  • nonbulbar conjunctival location (ie, plica semilunaris/caruncle, forniceal or palpebral conjunctiva)
  • increased tumor thickness
  • involvement of the eyelid margin
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: How is exophytic growth of a retinoblastoma defined?
pool.rationale: Exophytic retinoblastoma grows into the subretinal space. The exo- prefix in this instance indicates outward growth. Endophytic retinoblastoma grows into the vitreous cavity, the endo- prefix indicating inward growth.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Where are choroidal osteomas typically located?
pool.rationale: Choroidal osteomas are benign neoplasms composed of compact bone. They most commonly present as juxtapapillary, yellow-white subretinal masses with or without overlying retinal pigment epithelial changes. These lesions are marked by well-defined margins and low elevation and are unilateral in 75% of patients.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Intraocular calcification in the eye of a child is most diagnostic of what disease?
pool.rationale: Intraocular calcifications are the hallmark of retinoblastoma; they signify retinoblastoma until proven otherwise. In rare instances, intraocular calcifications can be seen in toxocariasis, persistent fetal vasculature, and Coats disease. In these cases, calcifications are usually focal and discrete, occurring within granulomas (toxocariasis) or a retrolental membrane (persistent fetal vasculature) or at the level of the RPE (Coats disease).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is a choristoma?

options.a: abnormal tissue in an abnormal location
options.d: normal tissue in an abnormal location

pool.rationale: A choristoma is a congenital anomaly in which there is normal, histiologically mature tissue in an abnormal location. Limbal dermoid is an example of this: normal, mature skin present in the abnormal location of the ocular surface. A hamartoma is an increased amount of normal tissue in a normal location. Capillary hemangioma is an example of a hamartoma: an increased number of capillary blood vessels in the normal location of the dermis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 65-year-old white woman with vitritis and negative treponemal antibody and interferon gamma release assay test results initially responds well to systemic corticosteroids; however, as the steroids are tapered, her vitritis becomes robust. A diagnostic and therapeutic pars plana vitrectomy is performed, and cytopathology discloses large, atypical lymphocytes with a large nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio. What is the approximate chance that she has or will develop intracranial lesions characterized by the same cells?
pool.rationale: The case described clinically is consistent with primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (PVRL). The cytopathology secures the diagnosis. In more than two-thirds of cases of PVRL, patients will have or will go on to develop intracranial disease. In fact, PVRL is a subset of primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL). Approximately 20% of patients with PCNSL (who do not yet have intraocular involvement) will go on to develop PVRL.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 62-year-old man presents with a palpable mass causing fullness of the upper lid. It has been progressing over 3 years. He denies pain or diplopia. A computed tomography (CT) scan reveals that the mass is well circumscribed and the globe is displaced down and toward the nose. What is the best next step in the management of this patient?
pool.rationale:
The most common epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland is pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumor). This tumor is pseudoencapsulated and grows slowly by expansion. Typically, the patient experiences no pain. Histologically, pleomorphic adenoma has a fibrous pseudocapsule and comprises a mixture of ductal-derived epithelial and stromal elements. Transformation into a malignant mixed tumor can take place in a long-standing or incompletely excised pleomorphic adenoma, with relatively rapid growth after a period of relative quiescence. Carcinomas, including adenocarcinoma (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma) and adenoid cystic carcinoma, can also develop in recurrent pleomorphic adenomas. To avoid recurrence and potential malignant transformation, the most appropriate management for this patient is lateral orbitotomy with excisional biopsy.
When a pleomorphic adenoma is suspected, incisional biopsy should be avoided. Fine needle biopsy of orbital masses may not adequately sample all representative areas of the tumor and lack tumor morphology, because it is difficult to make several passes at different angles through an intraorbital tumor. Observation is not the best management because long-standing pleomorphic adenomas can undergo malignant transformation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A glistening tan tumor is found on the inner surface of the pars plicata. Histopathology reveals proliferation of the nonpigmented ciliary epithelium. What is the diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
A Fuchs adenoma (also called pseudoadenomatous hyperplasia) is usually an incidental finding at autopsy and rarely becomes apparent clinically. It appears as a glistening, white or tan, irregular tumor arising from the inner surface of the pars plicata. It consists of benign proliferation of the nonpigmented ciliary epithelium with accumulation of basement membrane-like material.

Melanocytomas (magnocellular nevi) are benign tumors that may be located eccentrically on the optic nerve head, or on the iris, ciliary body, or choroid. Iris melanocytoma cells may seed the anterior chamber angle, thus causing glaucoma. Melanocytomas are composed of characteristic large, polyhedron-shaped nevus cells that have small nuclei and abundant cytoplasm filled with large melanin granules.

Ciliary body melanomas are comprised of spindle cells and/or epithelioid cells, not ciliary epithelium. Ciliary body nevi , which are usually small and incidentally found on histologic examination of globes enucleated for other reasons, are comprised of nevus cells without atypia or significant mitotic activity.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What anterior segment histological findings are characteristic of primary congenital glaucoma (PCG)?

options.a: hypertrophy of the ciliary muscle, trabecular meshwork, and Schlemm canal
options.b: endothelialization of the trabecular meshwork and anterior iris surface
options.c: hypoplastic scleral spur and an anomalous insertion of the ciliary muscle
options.d: neovascularization of the trabecular meshwork and anterior iris surface

pool.rationale: PCG is thought to be the result of arrested development of the anterior chamber elements. Histologically, the anterior chamber retains an immature conformation that is characterized by anterior insertion of the iris root, mesenchymal tissue in the anterior chamber angle, and a poorly developed scleral spur in which the ciliary muscle inserts directly into the trabecular meshwork. Hypertrophy of the ciliary muscle, trabecular meshwork, and Schlemm canal are not associated with PCG. Endothelialization of the trabecular meshwork and anterior iris surface is seen in iridocorneal endothelial syndrome. Neovascularization of the trabecular meshwork and anterior iris surface is present in many diseases associated with ischemia, including diabetes, central retinal vein occlusion, intraocular tumors, and ocular ischemic syndrome.

pool.q: How does corneal stromal healing differ from stromal healing in other tissues?
pool.rationale:
Corneal stromal healing is avascular. Healing in the corneal stroma occurs via the process of fibrosis rather than the fibrovascular proliferation seen in other tissues. The avascular aspect of corneal wound healing is critical to the success of penetrating keratoplasty as well as the various forms of refractive surgery.

Stromal keratocytes, fibroblast-like cells (also known as fibrocytes), are activated following a central corneal wound and eventually migrate across the wound, laying down collagen and fibronectin. In full-thickness corneal wounds, the endothelial cells adjacent to the wound slide across the posterior cornea; few cells are replaced through mitosis.

pool.q: What histopathologic finding can distinguish the conjunctival from the corneal epithelium?

Treatment is surgical, with margins of at least 2 mm to 3 mm, with deeper dissection if necessary. Cryotherapy and topical agents (mitomycin C, 5-fluorouracil, and interferon alpha-2b) have also been effective as adjuvants or as primary therapy.

pool.q: What principle of corneal wound healing is responsible for the finding shown?

pool.q: A patient with severe, recurrent corneal erosions had bilateral corneal refractile branching stromal opacities and underwent penetrating keratoplasty to clear the visual axis. Subtle refractile lines, central and subepithelial ovoid white dots, and diffuse anterior stromal haze appear early in life and, in a corneal graft, these may be the first signs of recurrence. The typical branching refractile lines, so-called lattice lines, develop as the condition progresses and are best seen against a red reflex or with indirect illumination. These lines start centrally and superficially and spread centrifugally, becoming deeper. The stroma can take on a "ground-glass" appearance, but the peripheral cornea typically remains clear. Epithelial erosions recur often and may occur as early as the first decade of life.

The stromal deposits in granular dystrophy type II (Avellino dystrophy) consist of both hyaline and amyloid. Some of the deposits will stain positively with Congo red and other deposits will stain positively with Masson trichrome.

pool.q: What is the most common clinical presentation of primary intraocular lymphoma?

pool.q: What is the best management of patients with choroidal nevi?

options.a: Patients should return periodically for assessment of nevus dimensions to confirm the absence of growth.
options.b: Patients with typical choroidal nevi should have A- and B-scan ultrasonography to document basal dimensions and thickness.
options.c: Fluorescein angiography is needed for serial size comparisons.
options.d: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) measurements of lesions thicker than 1 mm should be made.

The recommended management of a choroidal nevus is photographic documentation of all lesions, optical coherence tomographic (OCT) measurement of lesions thinner than 1 mm, ultrasonographic measurement of lesions thicker than 1 mm, and regular, lifelong, periodic reassessment for signs of growth. Findings from fluorescein angiography are not diagnostic; choroidal nevi may either hypofluoresce or hyperfluoresce, depending on the associated findings.

For typical choroidal nevi without observable elevation on ophthalmoscopy, A- and B-scan ultrasonography to document basal dimensions and thickness is not necessary. Likewise, fluorescein angiography is not needed for serial size comparisons, although baseline fundus photography can be useful for future comparison. Although optical coherence tomography (OCT) can be useful to measure the thickness of atypical nevi, it is not a substitute for ultrasonography, which generally provides more accurate thickness measurements along with the demonstration of internal reflectivity.

pool.q: What is the survival rate of patient with retinoblastoma confined to the retina if they receive appropriate treatment?
pool.rationale:
When retinoblastoma is contained within the eye, survival rates exceed 90%, compared to less than 50% if extraocular spread has occurred. Treatment strategies must consider preservation of life over preservation of the eye or vision. Enucleation is therefore associated with the best survival rates if the retinoblastoma has not spread and is appropriate when more than 50% of the globe is involved, orbital or optic nerve involvement is suspected, or if the anterior segment is involved. Enucleation techniques must minimize the risk of inadvertent perforation of the globe, and yet should obtain the greatest possible length of optic nerve. Globe-sparing therapy includes external beam radiation, plaque therapy, and systemic and, more recently, intra-arterial chemotherapy. External radiation has been associated with delays in orbital development and an increased risk of secondary tumors in the radiation field, in addition to the increased general risk of secondary tumors associated with retinoblastoma.
Chemoreduction employs chemotherapy, followed by thermo- or cryotherapy as local consolidation, if necessary, and avoids external radiation. With chemoreduction, stages A (tumor less than or equal to 3 mm), B (greater than 3 mm without seeding), and C (subretinal and/or vitreous seeds limited to 3 mm from tumor) in the newer International Classification System for Retinoblastoma (ICSRB) have been shown to have success rates over 90%.

pool.q: What represents the tertiary vitreous?
pool.rationale:
The embryologic development of the vitreous is divided into 3 phases:
  1. Primary vitreous, which consists of fibrillar material, mesenchymal cells, and vascular structures (including the hyaloid artery, vasa hyaloidea propria, and tunica vasculosa lentis
  2. Secondary vitreous, which is composed of collagen fibrils and hyaluronic acid
  3. Tertiary vitreous, which is composed of lens zonular fibers

pool.q: For the pictured finding and associated pathology, what is the appropriate treatment?
pool.rationale:
The clinical photograph shows extensive conjunctival nodules. The pathology demonstrates classic noncaseating (ie, without central necrosis) granulomas, characterized by multinucleated giant cells. This is pathognomonic for sarcoidosis and the preferred treatment is immunosuppression with steroids or immunomodulatory medication.
Systemic antibiotics would be indicated for adult inclusion cysts from trachoma. Systemic antihistamines are of benefit for severe allergic conjunctivitis. Radiation may be beneficial for localized conjunctival lymphoproliferative disorders.

pool.q: What clinical finding is most suggestive that a pigmented choroidal lesion is a choroidal nevus rather than a choroidal melanoma?
pool.rationale: Although no single clinical factor is pathognomonic for benign versus malignant choroidal melanocytic lesions, 11%–58% of nevi have overlying drusen. This frequency increases with age of the patient. Thickness greater than 2 mm, subretinal fluid, symptoms, orange pigmentation, and peripapillary location are clinical risk factors for growth. Nevertheless, 6%–10% of nevi show orange pigment, and 9%–15% are associated with subretinal fluid.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is a clinical feature of a melanocytic choroidal lesion that is concerning for melanoma?

options.c: absence of drusen or degenerative retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) changes

pool.rationale:
Using the mnemonic "To Find Small Ocular Melanoma Doing IMaging" (TFSOM-DIM) can assist in detecting factors that increase the risk of choroidal nevi transforming into small choroidal melanoma. The TFSOM-DIM acronym encapsulates the following risk factors:
  • Thickness >2 mm (on ultrasound)
  • Fluid subretinal (on OCT)
  • Symptoms of vision loss (by VA testing)
  • Orange pigment (on autofluorescence)
  • Melanoma hollow (on ultrasound)
  • DIaMeter >5mm (by photography)
Choroidal nevi may occur in up to 10% of the population. The typical nevus appears as a flat or minimally elevated gray-brown lesion with indistinct margins. According to the Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study, a nevus (or freckle) is < 1 mm in thickness, < 5 mm in largest basal diameter. Tumors that are > 1 mm in thickness and > 5 mm in largest basal diameter are in the size range overlapping that of nevi and that of small melanomas.

pool.q: What degenerative lens change is caused by migration of lens epithelium along the posterior capsule, followed by enlargement or swelling of those epithelial cells?
pool.rationale: Posterior subcapsular cataract is a result of epithelial disarray at the lens equator, followed by posterior migration of the lens epithelial cells along the posterior capsule. As the cells migrate, they can enlarge to 5-6 times their normal size. These swollen cells are called bladder or Wedl cells. If they involve the center of the lens in the visual axis, they can cause significant decrease in vision.A duplication cataract occurs after injury to the lens epithelium. The lens epithelium undergoes metaplasia and forms anterior subcapsular fibrous plaques. Following the resolution of the inciting stimulus, the lens epithelium may produce another capsule that completely surrounds the fibrous plaque.The earliest sign of focal cortical degeneration is hydropic swelling of the lens fibers with decreased intensity of eosinophilic staining. Eosinophilic globules (morgagnian globules) accumulate in the slitlike spaces between the lens fibers. Ultimately, the entire cortex can become liquefied.Nuclear cataracts take on a subtle homogenous eosinophilic appearance and are difficult to assess histologically.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most likely location for metastasis from uveal melanoma?
pool.rationale: The liver is the primary organ involved in metastatic uveal melanoma, and liver involvement is commonly the first manifestation of metastatic disease. After the liver, metastasis can affect the lungs, bones, and skin. All patients require metastatic evaluation prior to definitive treatment of intraocular melanoma.

pool.q: Macular corneal dystrophy nonsulfated glycosaminoglycan deposits stain best with what histopathology stain?
pool.rationale:
Colloidal iron and Alcian blue stains highlight the nonsulfated glycosaminoglycan deposits that accumulate intracellularly in stromal keratocytes and endothelium and extracellularly in the stroma in macular corneal dystrophy.
Macular dystrophy is autosomal recessive and caused by mutations in the carbohydrate sulfotransferase 6 gene (CHST6) on chromosome 16. The deposits in macular dystrophy are poorly defined, with hazy intervening stroma, and involve the cornea limbus to limbus.
Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) is a general tissue stain the stains the nucleus blue and the cytoplasm pink. Congo red stains amyloid and is useful in lattice corneal dystrophy. Masson trichome stains collagen blue and is useful for granular corneal dystrophy.

pool.q: A conjunctival pigmented lesion is biopsied. What histologic feature indicates a risk of malignancy?

options.a: epithelial cysts in the substantia propria surrounded by pigmented cells
options.b: intensely pigmented dendritic melanocytes in the episclera
options.c: increased pigmentation in conjunctival epithelial cells
options.d: epithelioid melanocytes in the superficial epithelium

pool.rationale: Epithelioid morphology and migration into the superficial epithelium are consistent with atypical melanocytic proliferation and indicate a risk of malignancy. Epithelial cysts in the stroma are suggestive of a compound nevus. Increased pigmentation in the epithelial cells might be seen in complexion-­associated melanosis or conjunctival hypermelanosis/primary acquired melanosis without atypia. Intensely pigmented dendritic melanocytes in the episclera are a feature of oculodermal melanocytosis (nevus of Ota).

pool.q: A patient presents with an elevated lesion on dilated fundus exam. The B-scan is shown in Figure 1 and the A-scan is shown in Figure 2. What is the most likely lesion?
pool.rationale: This imaging is most consistent with a circumscribed choroidal hemangioma. These hemangiomas are usually orange, dome-shaped lesions that can be associated with exudative retinal detachments, which can affect vision if the fovea is involved. A-scan ultrasonography demonstrated high internal reflectivity, as illustrated in the photo. A choroidal detachment can sometimes be dome shaped but usually has low internal reflectivity. Choroidal melanoma demonstrates low internal reflectivity and can also demonstrate choroidal excavation. Choroidal osteomas often cause acoustic shadowing secondary to calcium.

pool.q: What histochemical stain would be useful in confirming a diagnosis of senile calcific plaque?
pool.rationale: Alizarin red stains calcium and is therefore useful in identifying lesions containing calcium, such as senile calcific plaques. Alcian blue, which stains mucopolysaccharides, is often used to identify the composition of corneal deposits in macular dystrophy. Calcofluor white and acridine orange can be employed for the identification of Acanthamoeba.

pool.q: A 34-year-old woman presents with a painless, eyelid bump that she first noticed several months ago. On examination, she has a nontender nodule near the eyelid margin. The pathology is shown. From what gland does this lesion arise?

options.d: meibomian glands, or less commonly glands of Zeis

pool.rationale:
The lesion described in this question most likely indicates a chalazion, which should be differentiated from a hordeolum. A hordeolum or stye is an acute, inflammatory process typically involving the glands of Zeis and occasionally the meibomian glands of the eyelid. A focal collection of neutrophils and necrotic debris forms at the site of infection. The condition is usually self-limiting. A chalazion is a chronic lipogranulomatous reaction to lipid secretions from the meibomian glands or less often, the glands of Zeis. Sebum discharged to surrounding tissues thus causes an endogenous foreign body reaction. Because solvents in routine processing dissolve the dispersed lipid, histologic sections show histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells surrounding clear spaces. Lymphocytes, plasma cells, and neutrophils are also often present. Sebaceous carcinoma can mimic recurrent chalazion, and thus recurrent chalazia should be biopsied.
The glands of Moll are modified sweat glands that open into eyelash follicles. The glands of Wolfring are accessory lacrimal glands located in the eyelid.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What imaging modality is most helpful in assessing an iris melanoma?
pool.rationale: High-frequency ultrasonography enables excellent characterization of iris tumor size and anatomical relationship to normal ocular structures. Anterior segment OCT may be helpful, but commercially available instrumentation often does not penetrate to the level of the posterior iris. Iris fluorescein angiography may show intrinsic vascularity, but this finding is of limited value. CT orbit is also of limited utility in assessing an iris tumor.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What finding is demonstrated in this specimen?
pool.rationale:
Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of inherited retinal disorders characterized by diffuse progressive dysfunction of predominantly rod photoreceptors, with subsequent degeneration of cone photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Histologically, marked photoreceptor cell loss and RPE migration into the retina in a perivascular distribution are apparent and correspond to the bone-spicule-like pattern seen clinically.
Drusen occur in age-related macular degeneration. Calcification occurs in retinoblastoma. Fibroglial membranes occur in combined hamartoma of the retina and RPE.

pool.q: A patient has bilateral stromal opacities that are fleck-like, with intervening stromal haze and extend from limbus to limbus. This is caused by mutation in what gene?
pool.rationale:
CHST6)


Macular corneal dystrophy (MCD), an autosomal recessive corneal stromal dystrophy, is caused by mutations in the carbohydrate sulfotransferase 6 gene (CHST6), located at 16q22. This dystrophy is characterized by diffuse stromal haze that extends from limbus to limbus and is associated with poorly demarcated focal opacities (macules).
Mutations in transforming growth factor beta-induced (TGFβI) (chromosome 5q31) result in abnormal keratoepithelin, an adhesion protein present in normal stroma. Reis-Bücklers dystrophy, lattice dystrophy types I and III, and granular dystrophy types I and II (Avellino dystrophy) are all caused by TGFβI mutations.
Mutations in UbiA prenyltransferase domain containing 1 (UBIAD1) cause Schnyder corneal dystrophy. The metabolic defect in stromal keratocytes leads to crystalline cholesterol deposition in the stroma.
The gelsolin gene (GSN) is responsible for an amyloid precursor protein. GSN mutation causes lattice dystrophy type II (Meretoja syndrome), a systemic amyloidosis.

pool.q: What is the approximate mortality rate for iris melanoma?
pool.rationale: Iris melanomas (figure) account for less than 10% of all uveal melanomas and are associated with a distinctly lower mortality rate (1% to 4%) than melanomas of the ciliary body and choroid. Most iris melanomas grow as elevated pigmented iris masses, but rarely they may be diffuse, producing heterochromia. The differential diagnosis includes iris nevus, cysts, foreign body, metastatic tumor, iridocorneal endothelial syndrome, juvenile xanthogranuloma, and other rare iris tumors or ciliary body tumors extending into the iris. Ultrasonic biomicroscopy is helpful in defining the extent and location of the iris mass and whether the ciliary body is involved. Growth involving the angle and trabecular meshwork up to 3 to 4 clock hours may be an indication for excision. Extrascleral extension, and seeding or secondary glaucoma require localized radiation therapy or enucleation. Risk factors for iris melanoma include fair skin color and light iris pigmentation. There is no relationship to ultraviolet exposure. The risk of uveal melanoma is increased in fairly pigmented patients with oculodermal melanocytosis. Iris melanomas are classified using the modified Callender classification. Most are spindle cell melanomas, compared to the mixed cell type, which is most common in choroidal melanomas. Biopsy may be helpful in difficult diagnostic situations.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common histopathologic finding in pterygium?
pool.rationale: The most common histopathologic finding in a pterygium is basophilic degeneration of collagen within the substantia propria, due to actinic damage. Squamous metaplasia, surface keratinization, and loss of goblet cells may be seen in a subset of pterygia, but it is not a universal finding. Nuclear hyperchromasia is a finding in ocular surface squamous neoplasia, which may occur in association with a pterygium, but is a neoplastic, not degenerative change. Eosinophilic deposits are characteristic histopathologic findings of amyloid deposits, not pterygium.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Hemangiopericytoma is considered a subtype of what kind of orbital mesenchymal tumor?
pool.rationale:
Solitary fibrous tumor (SFT) is the most common mesenchymal orbital tumor in adults. The superonasal orbit is a common site, and presentation can include proptosis, pain, diplopia, decreased vision, and epiphora.
Studies have shown that hemangiopericytoma, fibrous histiocytoma, and giant cell angiofibromas of the orbit share common histologic and immunophenotypic characteristics and may be classified as subtypes of orbital SFTs.
Varix is an abnormally enlarged thin-walled vein. An orbital cavernous hemangioma is a hamartoma, consisting of an encapsulated mass of mature venous channels. Meningiomas are central nervous system (CNS) tumors of meningothelial origin.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What symptom associated with a lacrimal gland mass is most likely to be caused by an adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC)?
pool.rationale: Pleomorphic adenoma (benign) and ACC (malignant) are lacrimal gland tumors that present with ptosis, proptosis, and orbital fullness. The major symptomatic distinction between these 2 tumors is the pain reported by patients with ACC, due to the tumor's tendency to erode adjacent bones and invade orbital nerves.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Mutation of what gene is associated with congenital aphakia?
pool.rationale:
FOXE3

Mutations in the FOXE3 gene are associated with anterior segment mesenchymal dysgenesis. Homozygous mutations in this gene have been associated with a number of ocular diseases, including congenital aphakia, sclerocornea, microphthalmia, and optic disc coloboma. Reports of heterozygous mutations causing less severe ocular diseases such as anterior segment dysgenesis (sometimes referred to as anterior segment mesenchymal dysgenesis), and Peters anomaly have been published.
RB1 gene encodes the pRB protein, a tumor suppressor protein that is associated with retinoblastoma. One function of pRB is to prevent excessive cell growth by inhibiting cell cycle progression until a cell is ready to divide. When the cell is ready to divide, pRB is phosphorylated, becomes inactive, and allows cell cycle progression.
MYC is a family of regulator genes and proto-oncogenes that code for transcription factors. Mutation of MYCN has been associated with the development of retinoblastoma.
Alport syndrome is associated with bilateral anterior lenticonus. This syndrome is inherited in an X-linked manner and is caused by mutations in the COL4A5 gene in 80% of cases. In the remaining cases the condition is caused by mutations in the COL4A3 or COL4A4 genes; it may be autosomal recessive, or rarely autosomal dominant.

pool.q: In a 25-year-old patient with biopsy-proven conjunctival carcinoma in situ, what additional testing should be requested?
pool.rationale: Ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN) is rare in younger patients, and its presence warrants an evaluation for systemic immunocompromise. Patients younger than 50 years who present with OSSN should be screened for HIV infection. Diabetes mellitus, liver disease, and thyroid disease are less likely to be related to the presence of OSSN in this age group.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What clinical finding is more common in Chandler syndrome compared to the other variants of iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome?
pool.rationale: Chandler syndrome is the most common variant of iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome. It is characterized by minimal iris changes and predominantly corneal and angle changes. Microcystic corneal edema in the absence of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) is more common in Chandler syndrome. Progressive iris atrophy, corectopia / polycoria, hole formation, and heterochromia are more common in essential iris atrophy. Iris nevi are seen in Cogan-Reese syndrome. Varying degrees of PAS formation occur in ICE syndrome, and these are usually present more anteriorly within the angle due to abnormal migration of endothelium over the angle.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The red deposits in this specimen are made of what material?
pool.rationale: The photo in the stem and Figure C is a Masson trichrome stain of granular corneal dystrophy type 1 (GCD1), which demonstrates the granular hyaline deposits staining brilliant red. (Figure A is clinical photograph, and Figure B is an H&E stain of GCD1.) In lattice corneal dystrophy type 1, amyloid deposits exhibit apple-green birefringence. Mucopolysaccharides will stain in macular corneal dystrophy. In Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy, the irregularly thickened Descemet membrane is studded with anvil-shaped guttae.

pool.q: What histopathologic description best characterizes a hamartoma?

options.a: abnormal amount of mature tissue at a normal location
options.b: abnormal tissue derived from all 3 embryonic germ cell layers
options.c: normal mature tissue at an abnormal location
options.d: stereotypic, monotonous new growth of a specific tissue phenotype

pool.rationale: Hamartomas are congenital anomalies formed by hypertrophy or hyperplasia of mature tissue in a normal location. An example of a hamartoma is a cavernous hemangioma. A choristoma consists of normal, mature tissue at an abnormal location and can contain 1 or 2 embryonic germ layers. A teratoma is a tumor consisting of abnormal tissue derived from all 3 embryonic germ cell layers. A stereotypic, monotonous new growth of a specific tissue phenotype represents neoplasia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the normal timeframe after an eyelid skin injury for myofibroblasts to actively contract to decrease the size of the wound?
pool.rationale: Approximately the third day after an injury to the eyelid skin, myofibroblasts derived from vascular pericytes migrate around the wound and actively contract, decreasing the size of the wound.

pool.q: What is the most prominent cell type found in the vitritis associated with bacterial endophthalmitis?
pool.rationale:
The vitreous is acellular and avascular, so it is not often a primary site of inflammation. However, it commonly becomes secondarily involved in inflammation of adjacent tissues. Vitritis is the presence of white blood cells in the vitreous, either benign or malignant. Vitreous inflammation due to infectious agents is referred to as infectious endophthalmitis.
In bacterial endophthalmitis, the vitritis consists predominantly of an infiltrate of neutrophils (polymorphonuclear leukocytes), which are acute inflammatory cells.
Epithelioid histiocytes represent granulomatous inflammation. Infectious causes of granulomatous inflammation include fungal, viral, or atypical mycobacterial etiologies.
T and B lymphocytes are chronic inflammatory cells. The vitreous infiltrate in noninfectious uveitis is typically composed of chronic inflammation, including lymphocytes. Along with T and B lymphocytes, granulomatous inflammation may also be present in noninfectious causes of uveitis or vitritis.
Eosinophils are commonly found in allergic reactions, but may be present in some chronic inflammatory processes, such as sympathetic ophthalmia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What percentage of patients with intraocular lymphoma will develop central nervous system (CNS) involvement?
pool.rationale:
Of patients who present with primary intraocular lymphoma (PIOL), 60% will develop CNS lymphoma.
PIOL is the most common and most aggressive type of lymphoma involving the eye. To differentiate it from primary uveal lymphoma, it is more accurately termed primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (PVRL). It is typically a large B-cell lymphoma with findings in the vitreous and retina. It usually presents as bilateral posterior uveitis in an older patient. Clinically, there are diffuse vitreous cells that may be associated with subretinal infiltrates, retinal vasculitis, or vascular occlusion, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) clumping. PIOL is associated with primary CNS lymphoma. Ocular symptoms and signs may occur before the CNS findings.

pool.q: What is the best way to submit a pathologic specimen suspicious for conjunctival lymphoma?

options.a: place biopsy in Michel fixative for direct immunofluorescence
options.b: submit for polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for human papillomavirus (HPV)
options.c: submit fresh tissue for flow cytometry

pool.rationale:
Both benign and malignant lymphoid lesions of the conjunctiva show a salmon pink appearance, with a flat, smooth surface and soft consistency.
In addition to histopathologic examination, the specimens can be evaluated by immunophenotypic analysis. This is achieved by either flow cytometry of the fresh, unfixed tissue or by immunoperoxidase staining. Molecular techniques to determine monoclonality by revealing either kappa or lambda light chain dominance may be employed.
Direct immunofluorescence microscopy is used to diagnose ocular pemphigoid; it demonstrates a linear deposition of immunoglobulin (Ig) G or IgA, or complement component 3 (C3), at the epithelial basement membrane.
Human papillomaviruses have been reported to cause conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasias.
Masson trichrome stain is used to stain the granular hyaline material in granular corneal dystrophy.

pool.q: Glaukomflecken are seen on examination. What is the histology and patient history?

options.a: gray-white fibrillar material from pseudoexfoliative glaucoma
options.b: necrotic lens epithelial cells and degenerated subepithelial cortex following angle-closure glaucoma
options.c: endothelial cells associated with Cogan-Reese syndrome
options.d: macrophages engorged with phagocytosed proteinaceous, eosinophilic lens material from phacolytic glaucoma

pool.rationale:
Glaukomflecken are composed of necrotic lens epithelial cells and degenerated subepithelial cortex that result from prolonged elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), as in acute angle-closure glaucoma.
Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is a systemic condition that is characterized by the production and progressive accumulation of a fibrillar material in tissues throughout the anterior segment and in the connective tissue of various visceral organs.
Iridocorneal endothelial syndromes, including Cogan-Reese, are acquired unilateral abnormalities of the corneal endothelium. All forms of ICE syndrome have epithelial-like metaplasia and abnormal proliferation of the corneal endothelium.
In phacolytic glaucoma, the trabecular meshwork becomes occluded by both the lens protein and macrophages that are engorged with phagocytosed proteinaceous, eosinophilic lens material.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For what clinical presentation would a biopsy, rather than excision, of a limbal mass presenting as an atypical pterygium be recommended?
pool.rationale:
Excisional biopsy rather than simple excision should be considered if the conjunctival lesion has features suspicious for ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN).
One of these features is leukoplakia, a white, flaky appearance of the lesion surface. Leukoplakia is due to production of excess keratin (hyperkeratosis) by the conjunctiva. Normal conjunctiva consists of nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium. Production of keratin by the conjunctiva suggests that these cells have become abnormal. This is not pathognomonic for OSSN, but it is worrisome for neoplastic change. Other concerning features include a gelatinous appearance of the lesion and presence of feeder vessels and/or tortuous vasculature. Size is generally not an indicator of potential malignant transformation. The development of pterygia is largely due to ultraviolet (UV) and wind exposure; it is not typically hereditary in nature.
If squamous neoplasia is suspected, excisional biopsy should be performed to confirm the diagnosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the preferred treatment for the condition shown in the figure?
pool.rationale: The image depicts a B-scan ultrasonogram of a choroidal melanoma. Enucleation is preferred because morbidity is greater following radiotherapy for a large choroidal melanoma (greater than 10 mm in thickness). The Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study and other reports in the literature showed that pre-enucleation irradiation does not improve survival in patients with a medium or large choroidal melanoma.

pool.q: According to the Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study, how does eye-sparing plaque brachytherapy for well-selected patients affect melanoma-related mortality?

options.a: It does not adversely affect morbidity and mortality.

pool.rationale: The Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study (COMS) confirmed several clinical features as being predictive of tumor growth (ie, orange pigment, larger tumor dimensions, lack of drusen, and lack of adjacent retinal pigment epithelium [RPE] changes). Most small choroidal tumors did not grow in 5 years. The study indicated a low risk of dying within 5 years from a small choroidal melanoma, even when not treated. COMS also demonstrated that enucleation and iodine brachytherapy are equally safe alternatives regarding life prognosis for management of patients with medium choroidal melanoma. The study also documented pre-enucleation irradiation does not improve survival in patients with a large choroidal melanoma.

pool.q: A 6-week-old child is brought to the clinic by his parents because of a 1 cm reddish mass on the left upper eyelid that prevents the eye from opening fully. It has grown rapidly since birth. What is the typical histopathologic appearance of this lesion?

options.a: well-developed capillary channels lined with plump endothelial cells in a lobular configuration
options.b: large, irregular cavernous spaces with thin, fibromuscular walls
options.c: spindle cells arranged in a loose syncytium with occasional elongated cells demonstrating cytoplasmic cross-striations
options.d: thickened, tortuous nerves with proliferation of endoneurial fibroblasts and Schwann cells

pool.rationale:
This vignette describes a capillary hemangioma. These hemangiomas usually appear at or shortly after birth as bright red lesions, grow over weeks to months, and involute by the time a child reaches school age. Intervention is reserved for those lesions that affect vision because of ptosis or astigmatism and can cause amblyopia. The histologic appearance is well-developed capillary channels lined with plump endothelial cells in a lobular configuration.
Spindle cells arranged in a loose syncytium with occasional elongated cells demonstrating cytoplasmic cross-striations is a description of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. Although rhabdomyosarcoma could also present as a reddish, rapidly enlarging eyelid lesion, the average age of onset is 5-8 years, not at birth. Large, irregular cavernous spaces with thin, fibromuscular walls is the histologic description of a cavernous hemangioma, an encapsulated, orbital lesion found in adults. Thickened, tortuous nerves with proliferation of endoneurial fibroblasts and Schwann cells is a description of plexiform neurofibroma, which is pathognomonic for neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 70-year-old woman presents with a left lower lid lesion. She has had multiple recurrent chalazia at the same location. Examination shows a yellowish lesion at the lid margin with loss of overlying eyelashes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Sebaceous gland carcinomas are highly malignant tumors arising from sebaceous glands of the eyelid. These tumors may masquerade as recurrent chalazia or as chronic unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis. More than 50% of cases are initially misdiagnosed. Because these lesions typically demonstrate pagetoid spread, wide excisional biopsy and map biopsy of the conjunctiva are typically required.
Merkel cell carcinomas are typically violaceous-appearing lesions of the upper eyelid. These lesions are highly malignant and portend a poor prognosis.
Oncocytomas are slow-growing cystadenomas arising from the ductal and acinar cells of the accessory and main lacrimal glands, and may present as reddish-brown caruncular lesions.
Rosacea is characterized by excessive sebum secretion with frequently recalcitrant chronic blepharitis. It can progress, leading to chronic conjunctivitis, severe stromal keratitis, marginal keratitis, sterile ulceration, episcleritis, or iridocyclitis. If properly treated, these lesions can resolve with few sequelae.

pool.q: What is the major advantage of flow cytometry compared to immunohistochemistry in clinical practice?

options.b: It shows the location and distribution of these cells in tissue.
options.c: It shows the percentages of particular cells in a specimen.
options.d: It minimizes the risk of sampling errors.

pool.rationale: Flow cytometry’s advantage is that it actually shows the percentages of particular cells in a specimen. Flow cytometry’s disadvantages are its failure to show the location and distribution of these cells in tissue and the possibility of sampling errors. Depending on the number of cells in the sample and on clinical information, the flow cytometrist chooses the panel of antibodies to be tested. Flow cytometric data should therefore not replace but be used as an adjunct to morphologic hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining and immunohistochemistry interpretation.

pool.q: A 65-year-old man notices progressive, painless visual loss in the left eye. Fundus examination reveals the lesion in the image. B-scan ultrasonography reveals diffuse, homogenous choroidal thickening with a crescent-shaped area of acoustically hollow extrascleral extension. What findings are expected on enhanced depth imaging optical coherence tomography (EDI-OCT)?

options.a: thickening in choroid with choroidal shadowing, choriocapillaris thinning, photoreceptor loss, and loss of external limiting membrane
options.b: placoid lesions with thickening of the inner choroid
options.c: amorphous nodular lesions at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)
options.d: thickened, lumpy, bumpy contour of the choroid; choriocapillaris compression; and overlying photoreceptor loss

pool.rationale:
Patients with uveal lymphoma typically notice painless, progressive vision loss. Ophthalmoscopically, the presence of multifocal creamy-yellow amelanotic choroidal lesions tends to be most helpful in establishing the diagnosis. Fluorescein angiography depicts variable findings in patients with uveal lymphoma involving the choroid; indocyanine green (ICG) angiography provides superior characterization. Classically, multiple scattered hypocyanescent lesions, which correspond to the area of choroidal infiltration by the lymphoma, are present. OCT, specifically EDI-OCT, reveals placoid or irregular lesions and thickening of the inner choroid, often associated with subretinal fluid. Biopsy confirmation should be targeted to the most accessible tissue. For isolated uveal involvement, fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) or pars plana vitrectomy with biopsy may be indicated. Dense lymphoid infiltrates are seen on histologic evaluation.
Although OCT findings are not diagnostic in primary vitreoretinal lymphoma, amorphous nodular lesions at the level of the RPE may be seen. In secondary metastasis to the uveal tract, OCT may demonstrate a lumpy, bumpy contour; choriocapillaris compression; and photoreceptor loss in the overlying retina. In choroidal melanoma, OCT may show shadowing of choroid, thinning of choriocapillaris, loss of photoreceptors, retinal edema, and loss of external limiting membrane.

pool.q: What is the most common intraocular tumor?
pool.rationale: While the most common primary intraocular tumor of adults is choroidal melanoma, the most common intraocular tumor overall is metastatic. Metastatic lesions are also the most common orbital tumor in adults.

pool.q: What optic nerve cells are phagocytes?
pool.rationale: Oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and microglial cells are all types of glial cells, which support the function of the central nervous system. Oligodendrocytes produce and maintain the myelin sheath of the optic nerve; astrocytes are involved with support and nutrition; and microglial cells (central nervous system [CNS] histiocytes) have a phagocytic function. The axons of retinal ganglion cells are contained within the optic nerve.

pool.q: What secondary complications are common in patients with the lesion depicted in the figure below?

options.a: retinal schisis cavities and macular degeneration
options.b: choroidal neovascularization and retinal pigment epithelial detachment
options.d: amblyopia and central retinal vein occlusion

pool.rationale:
The "tomato ketchup fundus" in the figure shows the bright red color typical of diffuse choroidal hemangioma. Ultrasonography would reveal a diffusely thickened choroid with the thickest portion often in the central retina. Retinal detachment may occur secondary to disruption of the retinal pigment epithelium. Diffuse choroidal hemangioma frequently is located ipsilateral to a facial hemangioma, usually as a component of a variant of Sturge-Weber syndrome. The tumor is composed of well-formed choroidal vessels, which give the fundus a uniform deep-red color that has been compared to that of tomato ketchup. Sometimes only the posterior pole is involved; in other cases, the entire fundus is affected.
Choroidal hemangiomas are usually asymptomatic in childhood. During adolescence or adulthood, the choroid sometimes becomes markedly thickened. Degeneration or detachment of the overlying retina may follow. No treatment has been proven to prevent or reverse such deterioration, but scattered application of laser photocoagulation may help.
Glaucoma is the most common and most serious ocular complication. It has been reported to occur in up to approximately 70% of patients with SWS. Causes of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) include elevated episcleral venous pressure, hyperemia of the ciliary body with hypersecretion of aqueous, and developmental anomaly of the anterior chamber angle. Involvement of the skin of the upper eyelid, choroidal hemangioma, iris heterochromia, and episcleral hemangioma increase the likelihood of glaucoma.
Onset of glaucoma can be at birth or later in childhood. SWS glaucoma is difficult to treat. Initial therapy with topical eyedrops can be effective, especially in cases of later onset. Surgery is indicated in early-onset cases and when medical treatment is inadequate. Adequate long-term control of IOP can frequently be achieved, but multiple operations are typically necessary. A particular risk of glaucoma surgery in SWS is intraoperative or postoperative exudation or hemorrhage from anomalous choroidal vessels; this complication is caused by rapid ocular decompression. The surgeon must exercise special care with implanted glaucoma drainage devices to prevent excessive early postoperative hypotony.
