pool.q: A well-circumscribed, encapsulated, lobular orbital mass is excised from a 45-year-old woman with a 6-month history of painless proptosis and diplopia. What pathologic findings are most likely?

options.a: basophilic cells arranged in a cribriform (Swiss cheese) pattern
options.b: large vascular channels with intervening, delicate, fibrous tissue
options.c: spindle cell tumor in a loose syncytium with occasional cells bearing cross-striations
options.d: staghorn vascular pattern with densely packed oval- to spindle-shaped cells

pool.rationale:
Cavernous hemangiomas of the orbit are encapsulated tumors composed of large vascular spaces with intervening fibrous stroma. Symptoms commonly include painless proptosis and diplopia.
Adenoid cystic carcinoma is composed of basophilic cells commonly in a cribriform pattern, although other patterns can be seen. Staghorn vascular pattern with densely packed oval- to spindle-shaped cells is seen in some solitary fibrous tumors formerly known as hemangiopericytomas. Spindle-cell tumor in a loose syncytium with occasional cells bearing cross-striations would be found in a rhabdomyosarcoma. Adenoid cystic carcinoma, solitary fibrous tumor (hemangiopericytoma), and rhabdomyosarcoma are unencapsulated tumors that frequently present with pain.

pool.q: What ultrasound finding is suggestive of melanoma?

pool.q: What ocular fundus finding identifies the carriers of Gardner syndrome?

pool.rationale: RPE lesions mimicking CHRPE may be present in Gardner syndrome, a subtype of familial adenomatous intestinal polyposis. Histologic study of the RPE changes in Gardner syndrome reveals that they are more consistent with hyperplasia (increase in the number of cells) of the RPE than with hypertrophy. The presence of 4 or more of these lesions in each eye of a patient with a family history of Gardner syndrome or the APC mutation identifies that patient as a carrier of the gene mutation. These patients have a significantly increased risk for the development of colon cancer. In combined hamartoma of the retina and RPE, the RPE is hyperplastic and frequently migrates into the retina in a perivascular location. Vitreous condensation and fibroglial proliferation can be present on the surface of the tumor. Neoplasia (adenoma and adenocarcinoma) of the RPE is very rare. Osseous metaplasia of the RPE with bone formation can be a prominent feature in phthisis bulbi.

pool.q: For what intraocular tumor is fine-needle aspiration biopsy typically avoided, due to concern for tumor seeding?

options.d: adenocarcinoma of the retinal pigment epithelium

Intraocular fine-needle aspiration biopsy may be used for evaluation of uveal tumors, specifically if the diagnosis is uncertain (based on less-invasive evaluation methods) or when genetic evaluation (to clarify prognosis, such as in the case of uveal melanoma) is desired.
Due to concerns for tumor seeding, fine-needle aspiration biopsy is avoided if retinoblastoma is suspected. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy is not thought to pose significant risk for seeding of the other tumors listed (uveal melanoma, melanocytoma of the ciliary body, adenocarcinoma of the retinal pigment epithelium).

pool.q: What is the normal depth of the anterior chamber?
pool.rationale: The anterior chamber is bound anteriorly by the corneal endothelium, posteriorly by the anterior surface of the iris-ciliary body and pupillary portion of the lens, and peripherally by the trabecular meshwork. The normal depth of the anterior chamber is approximately 3.0–3.5 mm.

pool.q: What is the most common initial therapy for ciliary body medulloepithelioma?
pool.rationale: Medulloepithelioma often presents in an advanced state, with erosion into the anterior chamber and iris root, as well as neovascular glaucoma. In addition, these tumors can harbor malignant features, so management of medulloepithelioma usually consists of enucleation. Unlike its highly malignant counterpart in the CNS, as long as the tumor has not spread beyond the eye, intraocular medulloepithelioma has a good prognosis. Treatment options for ciliary body medulloepithelioma might also include cryotherapy, local resection, and plaque or external-­beam radiation therapy. The role of systemic or intravitreal chemotherapy in the treatment of ciliary body medulloepithelioma is not well established. Cryotherapy can be used for smaller or recurrent tumors. Local resection of medulloepithelioma is associated with tumor recurrence in 50%–100%. Standard-­dose external-­beam radiotherapy shows a mild response, but plaque radiation therapy is an alternative for smaller tumors. For larger tumors, enucleation is the preferred method of treatment.

pool.q: What is a typical histologic feature of posterior subcapsular cataract?

options.b: posterior migration of lens epithelial cells
options.c: infiltration of the posterior lens by inflammatory cells

pool.rationale: Normally, lens epithelial cells are present along the inner surface of the anterior lens capsule and terminate at the lens equator. When the equatorial lens epithelial cells migrate posteriorly onto the posterior lens capsule, they swell 5–6 times their normal size and become bladder cells (also called Wedl cells), resulting in the clinical appearance of posterior subcapsular cataract.

pool.q: What is the treatment of choice for symptomatic circumscribed choroidal hemangiomas?
pool.rationale:
A circumscribed choroidal hemangioma typically occurs in patients sporadically, without any systemic association. In some cases, the tumors produce a secondary exudative retinal detachment that often extends into the foveal region, resulting in blurred vision and metamorphopsia. Asymptomatic choroidal hemangiomas require no treatment. The most common indication for treatment is exudative detachment of the retina with fluid tracking towards the fovea.
The primary treatment of choice for symptomatic circumscribed choroidal hemangioma is photodynamic therapy (PDT). Historically, laser photocoagulation was used but was often unsuccessful and created scars; moreover, recurrent detachments were common. External beam radiotherapy is used for treating diffuse choroidal hemangiomas. To date, there is little published evidence to support the use of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitors to treat choroidal hemangiomas.

pool.q: A 70-year-old woman with a recurrent chalazion is referred to an ophthalmologist. She has an erythematous, nodular lesion on her upper eyelid. On closer examination, the ophthalmologist notes associated eyelash loss. What is appropriate management of this lesion?

options.b: warm compresses and topical antibiotic ointment
options.d: wide local excision with permanent margins

pool.rationale:
Sebaceous cell carcinoma most often involves the upper eyelid of elderly patients (40+). It is more common in women and in people with Asian ancestry. It can arise from meibomian glands, Zeis glands, or sebaceous glands in the caruncle. The lesion can mimic a chalazion or chronic blepharoconjunctivitis, so misdiagnosis is common. Histology shows foamy, lipid-laden cytoplasm. Poorly differentiated tumors can be difficult to distinguish from other epithelial lesions, and lipid stains such as oil red O or Sudan black B can aid diagnosis. However, these stains must be performed on tissue prior to processing. For this reason, wet tissue should be saved if sebaceous cell carcinoma is a concern.
A characteristic feature of sebaceous cell carcinoma is pagetoid spread or dissemination of individual tumor cells and clusters of tumor cells within epidermis or conjunctival epithelium. Tumor cells can also completely replace conjunctival epithelium, and this growth pattern is referred to as sebaceous carcinoma in situ. Sebaceous cell carcinoma spreads by direct extension, but node and distant metastases are possible. Factors associated with poor prognosis are upper lid origin, large size (> 10 mm), meibomian gland involvement, late excision, infiltrative growth pattern, poor sebaceous differentiation, pagetoid invasion, and lymphatic, vascular, and orbital invasion. Treatment recommendations include wide local incision with permanent margins. Frozen sectioning or Mohs microsurgery is suboptimal because of difficulty in identifying intraepithelial spread. Large or deeply invasive tumors may require exenteration.

pool.q: What is the most common precursor of squamous cell carcinoma of the eyelid?
pool.rationale:
Actinic keratosis is considered a precursor lesion to squamous cell carcinoma. Clinically, lesions appear as scaly, red macules or papules on sun-exposed skin in middle-aged to elderly individuals. Suspicious lesions should be biopsied and closely followed.
Keratoacanthoma is now thought to be a variant of well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. It often spontaneously involutes. If there is invasion through the basement membrane, then the lesion should be considered invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
Seborrheic keratosis and papilloma are both benign lesions.

pool.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with rapid left-sided proptosis. Imaging reveals an orbital tumor with bony destruction. In what gene is translocation likely implicated in this tumor?
pool.rationale:
FOXO1

In rhabdomyosarcoma, which is the most common orbital malignant tumor in childhood, proptosis is often sudden and progresses rapidly, requiring emergency treatment. Rhabdomyosarcomas arise from primitive mesenchymal cells that differentiate toward skeletal muscle. There are 3 recognized histologic types of orbital rhabdomyosarcoma: embryonal (most common), alveolar (worst prognosis), and pleomorphic (best prognosis). Histologically, spindle cells are arranged in a loose syncytium with occasional cells bearing ­cross-­striations. These cross-­striations are found in about 60% of embryonal rhabdomyosarcomas. Cytogenetic studies are important for identifying translocations such as FOXO1, which has prognostic implications. PITX1 mutations are associated with upper and lower limb deformities (club foot, Liebenberg syndrome). PAX6 mutations are associated with developmental ocular malformations (aniridia, Peters anomaly). GLC1 mutations are associated with primary ­open-­angle glaucoma.

pool.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a scaly, flat lesion on the eyelid. Biopsy and subsequent pathology of the lesion reveals thickened epidermis with atypia and solar elastosis of the underlying dermis. What is the risk of development of squamous cell carcinoma?

options.c: all lesions are considered early stage of squamous cell carcinoma
options.d: no chance of development of squamous cell carcinoma

pool.rationale:
Actinic keratosis is a precancerous squamous lesion appearing clinically as an erythematous or scaly macule or papule. Lesions most commonly occur in middle age on sun-exposed areas. Histologically, there are 5 subtypes that all display epidermal changes, such as acanthosis (epidermal thickening), hyperkeratosis (excess surface keratin layer), and parakeratosis (retained pyknotic nuclei with absence of granular layer). Epithelial dysplasia or partial thickness replacement by atypical cells is present and can range from mild to carcinoma in situ. Basal mitotic figures may be present. The underlying dermis displays solar elastosis similar to the elastotic degeneration seen in pinguecula or pterygium.
Squamous cell carcinoma may develop from underlying actinic keratosis (although most studies indicate the risk is less than 15%), and thus suspicious lesions should be biopsied. The base of the lesion must be examined to determine the presence of squamous cell carcinoma, and for this reason, shave biopsy is contraindicated. When squamous cell carcinoma does develop, however, there is a very low risk of metastasis compared to risk of metastasis from squamous cell carcinoma arising de novo.

pool.q: What type of cell proliferation is the most common clinical application for flow cytometry?
pool.rationale: Flow cytometry is most commonly used in clinical pathology for immunophenotyping hematopoietic proliferations. It may be performed on vitreous, aqueous, or ocular adnexal tissue specimens. Cells analyzed by flow cytometry must be sent as fresh (unfixed) specimens.

pool.q: What conjunctival finding is shown in the figure?
pool.rationale:
Conjunctivitis can be classified based on several features including chronicity (acute vs chronic); morphologic appearance (papillary vs follicular); and presence of membranes/pseudomembranes, cicatricial changes, or granulomatous inflammation.
The figure depicts (a) the clinical appearance of papillary conjunctivitis, along with (b) its histologic appearance, with closely packed, flat-topped papillae with central fibrovascular cores (arrows).
Follicular conjunctivitis is characterized clinically by small, pink, dome-shaped nodules without a clear central vessel. Granulomatous conjunctivitis may appear clinically similar to follicular conjunctivitis, and conjunctival biopsy may be used to confirm the diagnosis. Pyogenic granulomas on the conjunctiva appear clinically as red, elevated, pedunculated nodules and are formed by granulation tissue (not, in fact, granulomatous inflammation).

pool.q: What complication due to choroidal osteoma most commonly leads to visual loss?
pool.rationale: Choroidal osteomas are most common in the juxtapapillary location, and vision loss can occur due to development of subretinal neovascularization. Choroidal osteomas are benign tumors. Vitreous hemorrhage and retinal neovascularization are not associated with choroidal osteomas.

pool.q: What intraocular tumor frequently occurs in conjunction with central nervous system (CNS) involvement?
pool.rationale:
Primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (PVRL) or primary intraocular lymphoma (PIOL) is also referred as non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the CNS. More than half of patients presenting with ocular findings have or will develop involvement of the CNS.
Simultaneous brain and ocular metastasis may happen but are not thought to be directly related. A single case report is present in the literature describing such an event.
Uveal lymphoma is divided into primary and secondary categories based on the presence or absence of systemic lymphoma at the time of ocular presentation. The observed relationship between bilateral ocular involvement and systemic lymphoma is not limited to choroidal (uveal) lymphoma and has been reported for ocular adnexal and orbital lymphoproliferative tumors.
Retinoblastoma may invade the central nervous system. Trilateral retinoblastoma presents with bilateral tumors and pinealblastoma. The incidence of pinealblastoma among children with bilateral retinoblastoma is 6%.

pool.q: What type of lesion is an epibulbar dermoid an example of?
pool.rationale: An epibulbar dermoid is an example of a choristoma, a lesion composed of normal mature tissue in an abnormal location. A hamartoma is an exaggerated hypertrophy and hyperplasia of mature tissue in a normal location; an example of a hamartoma is a cavernous hemangioma, an encapsulated mass of mature venous channels in the orbit. Neoplasia describes unregulated growth of cells that results in a tumor; neoplasia can be benign or malignant. Reactive lesions occur in response to a stimulus such as inflammation or trauma, for example, chronic inflammation can lead to reactive fibrosis.

pool.q: An ophthalmologist performs an incisional biopsy of a pigmented eyelid lesion and suspects a melanoma. What histopathologic features would be consistent with this diagnosis?

options.a: changes in cellular morphology related to location
options.b: nests of round melanocytic cells at or below the epidermal–dermal junction
options.c: melanocytic cells growing within or around adnexal structure and vessel walls

pool.rationale:
Cutaneous melanoma is rare in the eyelids, but concerning histologic features include cytologic atypia with nuclear enlargement and hyperchromasia, atypical mitotic figures, pagetoid intraepidermal spread, and lack of maturation. Additionally, invasive melanoma may be preceded by a vertical growth phase, resulting in an elevated mass. A bandlike lymphocytic host response along the base of a mass lesion is more common in melanoma. Superficial spreading melanoma displays a radial intraepidermal growth pattern beyond the invasive component.
Melanocytic nevi are benign proliferations of melanocytic cells. They may occur at birth (congenital) or develop later in life. Histologically, most nevi are composed of specialized melanocytic cells that are round in shape and cluster in nests. The cytoplasm contains variable amounts of melanin. These cells tend to grow within or around adnexal structures, vessel walls, and the perineurium. Nevi are classified as junctional, intradermal, or compound.
Junctional nevi are flat, pigmented lesions. Histology demonstrates nests of melanocytes confined to the epidermal–dermal junction. With age, nevus cells migrate into the underlying dermis. Intradermal nevi display nevus cells confined to the dermis. Compound nevi have components of both junctional and intradermal nevi. Intradermal nevus cells display polarity or an evolution in cytomorphology.
Superficial nevus cells (type A) are polygonal or epithelioid in shape. Type B cells in the mid dermis are smaller, have less cytoplasm, and resemble lymphocytes. Type C cells of the lower dermis are spindle shaped. This maturation is useful in classifying melanocytic neoplasms as benign.

pool.q: A 47-year-old woman comes in for a routine eye examination. She is found to have the lesion in the photograph. The intraocular pressure in the same eye is 36 mm Hg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The most likely diagnosis is iris melanoma. The majority of iris melanomas occur in the inferior sector and many are associated with glaucoma. This lesion is pigmented and imaging confirms significant thickening in the area of the lesion. Iris nevi cause minimal distortion of iris architecture and are less likely to be associated with unilateral glaucoma.
Juvenile xanthogranulomas are rare lesions that typically occur in children and are associated with spontaneous hyphema. Melanocytomas are jet-black lesions that can occur anywhere in the uveal tract, but most often are found in the peripapillary region.

pool.q: What ultrasonography finding is most likely with this clinical photo?

options.b: less than 1 mm of lesion thickness

pool.rationale:
The lesion pictured is a choroidal melanoma. Standardized ultrasonography is the most important ancillary tool for evaluating ciliary body and choroidal melanomas. Standardized A-scan ultrasonography usually reveals a solid tumor pattern with high-amplitude initial echoes and low-amplitude internal reflections (low internal reflectivity). B-scan examination provides information about the size (thickness and basal diameter), general shape, and position of intraocular tumors. B-scan ultrasonography is also the best technique for detecting posterior extrascleral extension associated with intraocular malignancies.

pool.q: For the past 4 months, a 60-year-old retired boat captain has had a lesion on his right eye, as shown. The lesion has been surgically removed. What virus has been identified as a risk factor for this lesion type?

Human papillomavirus (HPV) 16 and 18 have been associated with CIN, as well as sessile papillomas, whereas HPV 6 and 11 have been associated with pedunculated papillomas. pool.q: A patient presents for blurry vision and is noted to have a change in refraction. Slit lamp examination also reveals a large and engorged episcleral vessel, and gonioscopy shows a pigmented lesion in 1 clock hour of the iridocorneal angle. What is the most likely cause of the refractive change?
pool.rationale: Because of their location behind the iris, ciliary body melanomas often remain asymptomatic until they become rather large. Patients may note reduced vision from induced astigmatism when the tumor touches the lens (ie, lenticular astigmatism); this can also result in cataract formation. Additional signs and symptoms include episcleral sentinel vessels; photopsia and visual field alterations from associated retinal detachment; and, rarely, secondary glaucoma. Corneal astigmatism is unlikely to result from a ciliary body melanoma but may be caused by ocular surface neoplasia. Orbital tumors flattening the posterior surface of the globe may induce axial hyperopia. Axial myopia is unlikely to develop in an adult with neoplasm.

pool.q: What is the likely cause of increased intraocular pressure in the setting of chronic vitreous hemorrhage?

options.c: "ghost cell" degeneration of red blood cells

pool.rationale: Red blood cells (RBCs) in the vitreous cavity may undergo degenerative changes. Clots undergo fibrinolysis and RBCs may diffuse throughout the vitreous after 3 to 10 days, with the development of RBC degeneration. Hemoglobin leaks from the RBC change the normally biconcave pliable cells to spherical, hollow, khaki-colored, less-pliable "ghost" cells (figure). These may have small fragments of denatured hemoglobin adherent to the inner surface of the cytoplasmic membrane (Heinz bodies). These spherical ghost cells may remain in the vitreous cavity for months and may occlude the trabecular meshwork by passing into the anterior chamber, leading to ghost cell glaucoma. Aspiration of the anterior chamber can confirm the diagnosis with the demonstration of ghost cells with the Heinz bodies. Longer-term findings with the degeneration of vitreous RBCs include macrophage phagocytosis and cholesterol crystal formation from the lipids of the cell membranes, at times provoking areas of fibrous and foreign-body, giant-cell reaction. The cholesterol crystals are freely mobile within the vitreous, which is often degenerated and liquefied after a hemorrhage, leading to cholesterolosis bulbi.

pool.q: What retinal tumor occurs in patients with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome?

Diffuse choroidal hemangiomas occur in patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome, and astrocytic hamartomas occur in tuberous sclerosis complex. The nevus flammeus or port-wine mark (previously port-wine stain) also occurs in Sturge-Weber Syndrome.

pool.q: What is the most common finding on eye examination in patients with leukemia?
pool.rationale: Retinal hemorrhages, typically ­white-­centered hemorrhages, are the most common ocular manifestation of leukemia. Patients with leukemia and retinal hemorrhages typically have anemia and thrombocytopenia. The other findings listed are much less common.

pool.q: An 8-year-old child presents with rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis. Biopsy shows spindle cells arranged in a loose syncytium with occasional elongated cells demonstrating cytoplasmic cross-striations, positive for desmin, vimentin, and myogenin on immunohistochemistry evaluation. What is the recommended primary treatment for this lesion?
pool.rationale:
Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary malignant orbital tumor of childhood (average age at onset is 5–8 years). The typical presentation is a child with rapid-onset, progressive unilateral proptosis. Due to the extremely rapid growth of the tumor, these patients require immediate attention, with urgent imaging and biopsy. There is often reddish discoloration of the eyelids that is not accompanied by local heat or systemic fever, as it is in orbital cellulitis. Orbital rhabdomyosarcoma has a better prognosis (overall 5-year survival rate of about 90%) than does rhabdomyosarcoma occurring in other body sites. Rhabdomyosarcoma arises from primitive mesenchymal cells that differentiate toward skeletal muscle. There are 3 recognized histologic types of orbital rhabdomyosarcoma: embryonal (most common), alveolar (worst prognosis), and pleomorphic (best prognosis, least common).
Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma may develop in the conjunctival stroma and may present as grapelike submucosal clusters (ie, botryoid variant). Histologically, spindle cells are arranged in a loose syncytium with occasional elongated cells demonstrating cytoplasmic cross-striations. These cross-striations are found in approximately 60% of embryonal rhabdomyosarcomas. Well-differentiated rhabdomyosarcomas feature numerous cells with well-defined cross-striations. Immunohistochemically, rhabdomyosarcoma typically is positive for desmin, muscle-specific actin, vimentin, and myogenin.
Before 1965, the standard treatment for orbital rhabdomyosarcoma was orbital exenteration, and the survival rate was poor. pool.q: What immunohistochemical stain is helpful in identifying lesions that arise from cells with a neuroectodermal origin?
pool.rationale:
Immunohistochemical stains are widely used in ophthalmic pathology. They take advantage of the specific antigens produced by specific types of cells. An antibody to a specific antigen is linked to a chromogen or color. When the stain is applied, the antibody binds to the cells that produce that specific antigen and the cell is stained by the chromogen.
Different antibodies can be used to identify different cell types and the lesions that arise from them. For example, epithelial cells produce cytokeratins. Therefore, a cytokeratin immunohistochemical stain can be used to identify adenomas or carcinomas which arise from epithelial cells.
S-100 is an antigen produced by cells that arise from neuroectoderm. The nervous system arises from neuroectoderm, including the retina and optic nerve. Neural tumors such as schwannomas or neurofibromas stain with S-100. Melanocytes also arise from neuroectoderm, so melanocytic lesions are positive with S-100 as well.
HMB-45 and Melan-A are more specific stains for melanocytes and melanocytic lesions. These stains are positive in nevi, primary acquired melanosis, and melanoma. But unlike S-100, they will not stain tumors of neural origin.
CD antigens are used to subtype white blood cells. T-cells stain with CD3 and B-cells with CD20. This is helpful in diagnosis of reactive lymphoid hyperplasia or lymphoma.
Actin, desmin, and myoglobin are used for lesions with smooth or skeletal muscle features, including leiomyoma or rhabdomyosarcoma.

pool.q: What mechanism best describes the pathophysiology of posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC)?

options.a: sequestration of proliferating lens fibers in the equatorial region
options.b: metaplastic transformation of epithelial cells into fibroblast-like cells
options.c: continual production of lens fibers leading to mechanical compression
options.d: posterior migration of lens epithelial cells

pool.q: A 6-year-old child presents for evaluation of unilateral decreased vision and redness of the right eye. What is the growth pattern most consistent with this clinical scenario?

Overall, retinoblastoma is typically diagnosed within the first year of life, with roughly 90% of cases being diagnosed before age 3 years.

Notably, there is no distinct tumor mass; instead there is infiltration of the retina, which makes the diagnosis challenging. These cases are also difficult because the view to the fundus is limited, and the typical calcification on ultrasonography or computed tomography (CT) imaging can be absent. Frequently, this variant may be misdiagnosed as endophthalmitis or uveitis, and it represents a childhood masquerade syndrome. While it can also present with tumor seeding into the anterior chamber and vitreous cells, the endophytic growth pattern describes growth on the retinal surface into the vitreous cavity and would present with visible tumor mass. Exophytic growth describes growth underneath the retina, and often presents with serous retinal detachment. Suppurative is not a characterized growth pattern of retinoblastoma.

pool.q: What is the most important component of the systemic evaluation of a patient with choroidal melanoma?

options.c: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain and orbits

Chest imaging may be with CT scan or chest x-ray.
Liver function tests are usually performed; however, they have recently become less reliable in the evaluation of liver metastases because of increasingly common fatty liver disease and the widespread use of cholesterol-lowering statins, which may alter liver enzyme levels. pool.q: An otherwise normal and healthy child presents with nonprogressive opacification and vascularization of the cornea probably caused by abnormal neural crest migration. What other finding is commonly associated with this presentation?

It can occur as an isolated abnormality but is more often associated with other ocular anomalies (eg, Peters), in which patients also have cornea plana. pool.q: The abnormal endothelial cells in the iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndromes show what unusual characteristics?

All are unilateral and eventually may develop glaucoma from a Descemet-like membrane covering the iris and angle. pool.q: What is the most common primary intraocular malignancy found in adults?

The most common secondary intraocular malignancy in adults is metastatic breast cancer in females and lung cancer in males. Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children but is extraordinarily rare in adults. Choroidal osteomas are choristomas and are not malignant.

pool.q: A 39-year-old asymptomatic Hispanic female patient is referred for evaluation of a lesion noted (see image). What is the most likely diagnosis?

pool.q: What is the most common primary site of systemic cancer in men that causes intraocular metastasis?
pool.rationale: The most common tumor occurring in the adult eye is a secondary metastatic tumor. This most frequently presents as a choroidal mass, disseminated from a carcinoma elsewhere in the body. In females, the breast is the most common primary tumor site; in males, the lung is the most common primary tumor site, accounting for 40% of solid tumors that metastasize to the uveal tract.

pool.q: Patients with ocular or oculodermal melanocytosis may have an increased risk of what tumor?

If there is associated cutaneous hyperpigmentation along the trigeminal nerve distribution, the condition is called oculodermal melanocytosis (nevus of Ota). These conditions may have associated melanocytosis of the meninges and orbit. Oculodermal melanocytosis is more common in Asian and African American populations, but uveal melanoma is rare in these groups and the incidence of melanoma is not increased with the presence of oculodermal melanocytosis. In white populations, however, the occurrence of ocular or oculodermal melanocytosis is associated with an increased risk of uveal melanoma. The pathology of the melanocytosis is increased dendritic melanocytes in the episclera, sclera, or dermal layers of the skin. Associated hyperpigmentation of the iris and choroid is another common finding. The lifetime risk of uveal melanoma in this group is about 1:400, much greater than the 1:13,000 incidence in the general white population. pool.q: What genetic mutation causes retinoblastoma to develop?

options.b: complete loss of 1 copy of the RB1 gene
options.c: trisomy of the long arm of chromosome 13
options.d: mutations in both copies of the RB1 gene

pool.rationale:
RB1 gene

Retinoblastoma develops when both copies of the retinoblastoma gene (RB1) become nonfunctional, either by a deletion error or by mutation. RB1 is located on the long arm of chromosome 13 and encodes for retinoblastoma protein, pRB, which functions as a tumor suppressor. Thus, loss of the gene does not actively cause tumorigenesis but rather leads to loss of tumor suppression, resulting in the development of retinoblastoma (and other tumors, such as osteosarcoma). A single normal gene copy is sufficient to suppress the development of retinoblastoma. However, when 1 abnormal gene is present, if a mutation in the remaining normal gene occurs during retinal differentiation, loss of tumor suppression occurs, and retinoblastoma is likely to develop.
A single-point mutation on chromosome 13 or even complete loss of 1 copy of the RB1 gene would not lead to retinoblastoma formation unless something were to happen to the second copy of the RB1 gene. Trisomy of the long arm of chromosome 13 is not associated with the development of retinoblastoma.

pool.q: What management is recommended for a patient who has newly diagnosed melanocytoma (magnocellular nevus)?

The pigmented lesions occur at the optic disc and often extend into the peripapillary retina and choroid. As they are generally benign lesions with an estimated 1% to 2% risk of transformation to malignant melanoma, observation is warranted in the absence of documented growth.

pool.q: When monitoring a choroidal nevus, ultrasonographic measurements should be performed for lesions greater than what thickness?

Fewer than 1% of lesions thinner than 1 mm are melanomas; however, more than 20% of choroidal melanocytic tumors thicker than 3 mm are melanomas. Tumors that are 1-3 mm in thickness are more difficult to classify; therefore, careful documentation of size and growth is important.

pool.q: What is the most frequent indication for frozen sections?
pool.rationale: A frozen section, tissue that is snap-frozen and immediately sectioned in a cryostat, is indicated when the results of the study will affect intraoperative management of the patient. Permanent sections, tissue that is processed into paraffin prior to sectioning, are always preferred in ophthalmic pathology because of the inherent small size of the samples and the superior morphological preservation achieved with this technique. If the tissue sample is too small, it could be lost during frozen sectioning. The most frequent indication for a frozen section is to determine whether the resection margins are free of tumor, especially in eyelid carcinomas. When tissue is submitted for margin evaluation, appropriate orientation of the specimen, correlated with documentation (through drawings of the excision site, labeled margins, or margins of the excised tissue that are tagged with sutures or other markers), is crucial. Two techniques can be used for assessing the margins in eyelid carcinomas (eg, basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma): (1) routine frozen sections; and (2) Mohs micrographic surgery, which preserves normal tissue while obtaining clear margins. Eyelid lesions, especially those located in the canthal areas, require tissue conservation in order to maintain adequate cosmetic and functional results.

pool.q: A 70-year-old woman who is undergoing treatment for gastric adenocarcinoma presents with a complaint of a dark brown lesions around her right eye. On examination, there are multiple, well-circumscribed, pigmented lesions with a greasy appearance. She reports the lesions occurred suddenly several months before her cancer diagnosis. What will the histologic specimen show?

options.a: a squamous lesion with central keratin-filled crater

options.d: fingerlike projections of epidermis surrounding a fibrovascular core

These lesions may be pigmented. Sudden onset of multiple seborrheic keratoses is known as the Leser-Trélat sign and is associated with systemic malignancy. Inverted follicular keratosis is irritated seborrheic keratosis. This appears as a cutaneous horn and histologically contains nonkeratinized squamous epithelial whirling or squamous eddies instead of pseudohorn cysts.
Papilloma refers to the growth pattern of fingerlike upward projections of epidermis surrounding fibrovascular cores. A squamous papilloma consists of keratinized epidermal fronds. A keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing epithelial proliferation. Histologically, keratoacanthomas are composed of an invagination of squamous cells, often filled with keratin. The rapid proliferation of epithelial cells undermines adjacent skin.

pool.q: What is the main component of a dermolipoma?

Dermolipomas most commonly occur in the superotemporal quadrant, toward the fornix, and may extend posteriorly into the orbit. They also contain dermal adnexal structures, including hair follicles and sebaceous glands, although these are not the main component.

The histologic features of complex choristomas overlap with those of epibulbar dermoids or dermolipomas. pool.q: What is the most common etiologic cause of non-syphilitic interstitial keratitis?
pool.rationale: The most common etiologic agent of non-syphilitic interstitial keratitis is the herpes simplex virus. Other organisms that can cause interstitial keratitis include Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mycobacterium leprae, Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease) and Epstein-Barr virus. Interstitial keratitis can be caused by either congenital or acquired syphilis, although cases associated with congenital syphilis are more common.

pool.q: What is the peculiar pathologic feature exhibited by the tumor cells of an optic nerve melanocytoma?
pool.rationale:
Melanocytoma is a darkly pigmented lesion, typically situated on or adjacent to the optic disc. It may extend into adjacent retina or posteriorly into the optic nerve. Melanocytomas are benign lesions and rarely have malignant transformation.
Histologically, melanocytoma is a magnocellular nevus with densely pigmented, plump, polyhedral melanocytes. The dense pigment obscures the cell detail, so bleach preparations are needed to see the cytologic features. The cells have small nuclei with small, regular nucleoli and abundant cytoplasm.

pool.q: What cells produce the collagen found in scar tissue?
pool.rationale: Wound healing consists of an acute inflammatory phase, regeneration, repair, and contraction. Neutrophils and fluid enter the extravascular space in the acute inflammatory phase. Macrophages remove debris from the damaged tissue, new vessels form, and fibroblasts begin to produce collagen. Epithelial cells contribute to regeneration, which is the replacement of lost cells. Regeneration only occurs in tissues composed of cells capable of undergoing mitosis throughout life. Repair is the process of restructuring of tissues that leads to a fibrous scar. Contraction is the final phase that causes the reparative tissues to shrink so that the scar is smaller than the surrounding uninjured tissues.

pool.q: An 85-year-old man presents with erythema and madarosis of the right eyelids. Incisional biopsy reveals foamy cells and pagetoid spread. A complete surgical excision is planned. What is the best histochemical stain to highlight these cells?

Because they reveal lipid within the cytoplasm of tumor cells, special stains, such as oil red O or Sudan black B, can be used to diagnose sebaceous carcinomas. Tissue staining for lipids should be performed on frozen or cryostat sections because the lipid constituents are often removed during paraffin processing. Another common histologic feature of sebaceous carcinoma is pagetoid spread, which involves the dissemination of individual tumor cells and/or clusters of tumor cells within the epidermis or conjunctival epithelium. The PAS reagent, which stains glycogen and proteoglycans, is useful for identifying basement membranes (eg, Descemet membrane, lens capsule) and ­mucin producing cells (eg, conjunctival goblet cells) in ocular tissues. ­Hematoxylin-­eosin is a general tissue stain that stains the nucleus blue and the cytoplasm ­pink-­red. Calcium phosphate salts are stained black with the von Kossa stain, as in band keratopathy.

pool.q: What is the most important risk factor for metastatic disease on histopathology of an enucleated globe from a patient with retinoblastoma?

Massive choroidal invasion, extrascleral extension, or postlaminar optic nerve disease increase the risk that metastatic disease could develop. pool.q: A 45-year-old man presents with recent onset of unilateral diplopia, proptosis, and a palpable orbital mass. Biopsy of the mass shows a staghorn vascular pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Histologically, the "staghorn" vascular pattern is present on 87% of fibrous tumors.
Lymphangiomas are congenital lesions that often present in childhood as fluctuating proptosis. Lymphangiomas are poorly circumscribed, diffusely infiltrating lesions.
Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary malignant orbital tumor of childhood. The average age of onset is 7-8 years, so it would be unlikely to be seen in a 45-year-old person.
Meningiomas are most often secondary lesions extending into the orbit from a primary intracranial lesion. Primary intraorbital meningiomas are usually intraconal, arising from the optic nerve sheath.

pool.q: What histopathologic corneal finding is present in cases of bullous keratopathy?
pool.rationale: Bullous keratopathy is characterized by extensive loss of endothelial cells that leads to decompensation, triggering Descemet folds, stromal edema followed by intracellular epithelial edema, and, ultimately, separation of the epithelium from the Bowman layer. Descemet membrane may be thickened and folded but it is not atrophic.

pool.q: Regarding the abnormality shown, what term applies to normal tissue present in an abnormal location?
pool.rationale:
A choristoma is a benign, congenital proliferation of histologically mature tissue that is abnormal for a given topographic location. Limbal dermoids (shown), a type of choristoma, are firm, dome-shaped, white-yellow nodules typically found at or straddling the limbus, most commonly in the inferotemporal quadrant.
Hamartomas are benign congenital proliferation, or abnormal overgrowth, of normally present tissue for a given location. For example, a capillary hemangioma of the eyelid is a hamartoma. A tumor that is made up of tissue derived from all 3 embryonic germ layers is called a teratoma (eg, an orbital teratoma). Sarcomas are malignant soft tissue tumors.

pool.q: What disorder is typically demonstrated by Langhans giant cells in histologic specimens?
pool.rationale: Multinucleated giant cells, including the Langhans giant cell, are characteristic of granulomatous inflammation and often observed in histologic specimens of sarcoid granulomas. Bacterial infections are characterized by acute inflammation and the presence of neutrophils. Lymphoma is a malignant lymphoproliferative process in which dense tissue infiltration of a monoclonal population of lymphocytes is typically present. The inflammatory infiltrate seen in orbital pseudotumor, also called nonspecific orbital inflammation, is composed of a mixture of acute and chronic inflammatory cells, including eosinophils, neutrophils, macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.

pool.q: What anatomic landmark marks the termination of Descemet membrane on gonioscopy?
pool.rationale: The termination of Descemet membrane is manifested gonioscopically as the Schwalbe line. The scleral spur, a triangular extension of the sclera, appears as a white band gonioscopically. The trabecular meshwork and the Schlemm canal are nested in the groove formed by the scleral spur and corneoscleral tissue. The iris root inserts posterior to the trabecular meshwork.

pool.q: What is the initial location of a ring melanoma?
pool.rationale: Ciliary body melanomas are not usually visible unless the pupil is widely dilated. Some erode through the iris root into the anterior chamber and become visible during gonioscopy or external examination. Eventually, the tumor extends through the sclera along aqueous drainage channels, producing an epibulbar nodule. Some ciliary body melanomas assume a diffuse growth pattern and extend up to 360 degrees around the eye; in this case, they are known as ring melanomas.

pool.q: An otherwise healthy 57-year-old man had a circumscribed reddish-orange lesion in the superotemporal retina. Histology of the lesion is shown in the figure. What is the diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The figure shows a large number of thin-walled, variably sized vessels within the choroid, with overlying retinal detachment. Choroidal hemangiomas may appear as predominantly capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas, or a mix of the 2. There may be compressed melanocytes, hyperplastic retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and fibrous tissue proliferation in the adjacent and overlying choroid. Circumscribed choroidal hemangioma typically occurs in patients without systemic disorders.
Histologically, posterior uveal melanomas are composed of spindle cells and/or epithelioid melanoma cells. Choroidal osteomas are located in the peripapillary choroid and, histologically, are composed of compact bone. Histology of neurilemomas or schwannomas reveals choroid infiltrated by spindle-shaped cells with slender, wavy nuclei.

pool.q: A 45-year-old woman presents for a routine evaluation. The figure shows a slit-lamp photograph of her right eye. What extraocular manifestation of this disorder would be likely?

options.b: a deforming arthritis of the distal joints

pool.rationale: The figure demonstrates sclera thinning without inflammation. This presentation is most consistent with scleromalacia perforans, a condition typically seen in patients with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. Manifestations of disease include a deforming arthritis of the distal joints. Episodes of shortness of breath can be seen in patients with sarcoidosis, another potential cause of scleritis, but not of scleromalacia perforans. Muscle spasms, weakness, tachycardia, and arrhythmias are not directly associated with this condition or rheumatoid arthritis.

pool.q: What is the critical finding in the diagnosis of phacoantigenic uveitis?
pool.rationale: Phacoantigenic uveitis results from a compromise or violation (usually traumatic or surgical) of the lens capsule that causes the exposure of lens material, thereby inciting a granulomatous anterior uveitis. Hypopyon, granulomatous keratic precipitates, and elevated intraocular pressure (by virtue of lens material or macrophages that have ingested lens material that can obstruct the trabecular meshwork) can all occur in phacoantigenic uveitis, but lens violation must first happen. If lenticular capsule has not been breached in some way, then another cause of the inflammation should be sought out.

pool.q: What location of a periocular lymphoma is associated with the lowest risk of systemic lymphomas?
pool.rationale:
It is important to understand the risk of systemic lymphoma in a patient with periocular lymphoma. More than half of periocular lymphomas involve prior, concurrent, or future systemic spread (20%-30% have previous or concomitant systemic disease, 30% develop it over 5 years). This risk is somewhat predicted by the site of periocular origin: The risk is lowest for conjunctival lesions, greater for orbital lesions and highest for eyelid lesions. Lesions in the lacrimal fossa may carry a greater risk than those occurring elsewhere in the orbit. Bilateral periocular involvement greatly increases the risk of systemic disease, but it is not a definitive sign of systemic disease. The risk of systemic disease is increased for decades after the original lesion is diagnosed, regardless of the initial lesion’s location.
The prediction of biologic behavior of periorbital lymphoproliferative lesions is limited, despite clinical, histopathologic, and immunohistochemical studies. Pathologically, lymphoproliferative lesions with lymphoid follicles with germinal centers, a polymorphous mixture of plasma cells, and mature lymphocytes favor a diagnosis of reactive lymphoid hyperplasia. More monotonous, small, round lymphocytes are seen in low-grade malignant lymphomas, whereas high-grade lymphomas demonstrate more malignant nuclei and frequent mitoses. Immunohistochemistry demonstrating mono- or polyclonality is helpful on tissue sections or by flow cytometry.

pool.q: What systemic condition is associated with retinal pigment epithelial hamartoma?
pool.rationale:
There is a strong association of hamartomas of the RPE (RPEH) and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), an autosomal dominant condition with nearly universal development of colon cancer. Gardner syndrome is the association of FAP with extracolonic manifestations, including cutaneous cysts, osteomas, odontomas, and extracolonic cancers. Multifocal areas of RPEH have been described in family members of patients with FAP. These may differ from congenital hypertrophy of the RPE (CHRPE) in that RPEH lesions are bilateral, more haphazard, and have irregular and jagged borders. The RPE lesions are detectable before the development of polyposis and carcinomas. The pathology of the pigment epithelial lesions in RPEH is a monolayer or multilayered mound of RPE cells, representing a hamartoma (increased amount of normal tissue in its normal location). FAP is associated with a mutation on 5q21. In contrast to RPEH, CHRPE is usually a solitary well-demarcated, flat, darkly pigmented subretinal plaque from 1 to 19 mm, located in the midperiphery, which may be heavily pigmented.
The earliest CHRPE plaques are noted in patients in the second decade. CHRPE is usually nonhereditary and sporadic. Areas of depigmentation (lacunae) within the lesion may be noted. A depigmented ring may surround the lesion. Mild growth of CHRPE has been documented. Histologically CHRPE consists of taller than normal RPE cells, densely packed with large, spherical melanin pigment granules. There is both hyperplasia and hypertrophy of the RPE, with degeneration of the overlying retina. The figures depict selected clinical findings of CHRPE.

pool.q: What kind of feature is more commonly seen in adult conjunctival papillomas than in pediatric conjunctival papillomas?
pool.rationale:
The most common ocular surface neoplasms are squamous in nature. Squamous papillomas may be divided into pedunculated and sessile types.
Pedunculated papillomas are exophytic, pink-red, strawberry-like fronds frequently localized to the caruncle, plica semilunaris, or forniceal conjunctiva. Pedunculated papilloma is associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, subtypes 6 and 11. They may spontaneously involute over months or years. Pedunculated papillomas typically exhibit benign behavior and rarely undergo malignant transformation.
A sessile papilloma generally arises on the bulbar conjunctiva, especially at the limbus, and occurs more commonly in adults. This type of papilloma is also associated with HPV infection, subtypes 16 and 18—the same subtypes associated with squamous malignancies.

pool.q: What is the etiology of this skin lesion?
pool.rationale:
Human papillomavirus may infect the skin of the eyelids, typically manifesting as verruca vulgaris, as seen in the photo. Clinically, verruca vulgaris is usually an elevated lesion with fine papillary projections. Histologically, the lesions exhibit a papillary growth pattern and demonstrate parakeratosis, hyperkeratosis, and acanthosis.
Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a member of the poxvirus family. Infections of the eyelid with the mite Demodex folliculorum is increasingly recognized as a cause of chronic eyelid and conjunctival inflammation. A hordeolum is typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

pool.q: A corneal scraping from a patient with keratitis demonstrates cysts and trophozoites. What is the etiology of the keratitis?

Acanthamoeba protozoa have a cyst morphology, and these cysts are difficult to eradicate from the corneal stroma. Less commonly, trophozoite forms might also be identified. Epithelial cells infected with herpesvirus might display intranuclear inclusions; these are rarely seen histologically because corneal grafting is not generally performed during the acute phase of infection. Pseudomonas is a ­gram-­negative bacterium and is rod shaped (bacillus).

pool.q: What other organs should the ophthalmologist be most concerned about in a patient with a retinal capillary hemangioma?
pool.rationale: Retinal capillary hemangiomas are a common disease manifestation of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome, wherein cerebellar and/or spinal hemangioblastomas may develop in patients but are less common. The VHL gene, which is located on chromosome 3, is mutated in the syndrome. Mutations in VHL cause overproduction of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and other hypoxia-inducible factors, leading to the development of highly vascular tumors. A number of other tumors and cysts may develop in patients with this syndrome, the most serious of which are renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.

pool.q: An 8-year-old girl presents with flat light-brown spots on the skin, benign skin growths, and encapsulated peripheral nerve tumors. Her father has similar findings. What feature would a biopsy of her optic nerve tumor most likely reveal?
pool.rationale: This girl and her father have neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Her peripheral nerve tumors are most likely representative of neurilemomas (also called schwannomas), which arise from Schwann cells. Neurilemomas have two histologic patterns. Antoni A spindle cells are arranged in interlacing cords, whorls, or palisades that may form Verocay bodies (collections of fibrils resembling sensory corpuscles). Antoni B pattern is made up of stellate cells that have a mucoid stroma. Optic nerve gliomas, which are frequently associated with neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1), most commonly present in the first decade of life and are ­low-­grade juvenile pilocytic astrocytomas. Enlarged, deeply eosinophilic filaments known as Rosenthal fibers, which represent degenerating cell processes, can be found in these ­low-­grade tumors. Psammoma bodies can be found in meningiomas. Staghorn vascular spaces are observed in hemangiopericytomas and related solitary fibrous tumors. Verocay bodies are collections of fibrils that resemble sensory corpuscles in the Antoni A spindle cell pattern observed in schwannomas (also called neurilemomas).

pool.q: What is the first-line treatment of choice for choroidal hemangioma-associated subfoveal detachment?

options.a: intravitreal vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitor

pool.rationale: The current treatment of choice for symptomatic circumscribed choroidal hemangioma is photodynamic therapy (PDT). Most choroidal hemangiomas respond to PDT, with resolution of the subretinal fluid and partial regression of the lesion, often with associated improvement in vision. However, cystoid macular edema may persist, particularly if chronic, and any degenerative changes in the overlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) may limit visual recovery; PDT may need to be repeated. Choroidal hemangiomas were traditionally managed with laser photocoagulation, which created chorioretinal adhesions. However, photocoagulation was often unsuccessful and created scars. Recurrent detachments were common. Low-dose radiation (via brachytherapy or external radiotherapy methods such as charged-particle, stereotactic, or external beam) has been successfully used to treat choroidal hemangiomas, including those unresponsive to PDT. For diffuse choroidal hemangioma, because of the diffuse nature of the tumor, external beam radiotherapy techniques, rather than plaque brachytherapy, are used. There is little published evidence to support the use of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitors to treat choroidal hemangioma.

pool.q: What inflammatory cells, when found aggregated together, are indicative of granulomatous inflammation?
pool.rationale:
Inflammatory cells characteristic of chronic inflammatory processes include monocytes and lymphocytes. Monocytes are classified as histiocytes or macrophages when they migrate from the intravascular space into tissue. Histiocytes have eccentric nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Some histiocytes are referred to as epithelioid histiocytes because of their resemblance to epithelial cells, with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and sharp cell borders. Epithelioid histiocytes may form a ball-like aggregate known as a granuloma, the hallmark of granulomatous inflammation.

Basophils contain basophilic intracytoplasmic granules; when found in tissues rather than in the blood, they are referred to as mast cells.

Neutrophils typify acute inflammatory cells and can be recognized by their multisegmented nucleus and intracytoplasmic granules. They are usually associated with bacterial infections and may be found in blood vessel walls in some forms of vasculitis.

Lymphocytes are cells characteristic of chronic inflammation. They are small with round, hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm. They either mature in the thymus (T cells) or bone marrow (B cells). B cells may produce immunoglobulin and differentiate into plasma cells that are characterized by eccentric "cartwheel" or "clockface" nuclei and a perinuclear halo corresponding to the Golgi apparatus. These cells may become completely distended with immunoglobulin and form Russell bodies.

pool.q: What growth pattern of retinoblastoma is most likely to cause an exudative retinal detachment?
pool.rationale:
The 3 growth patterns of retinoblastoma are endophytic, exophytic, and diffuse infiltrative. In the endophytic growth pattern, the tumor appears as a white or cream-colored mass that breaks through the internal limiting membrane. Endophytic retinoblastoma can be associated with vitreous seeding. Exophytic tumors are yellow-white and occur in the subretinal space. Exophytic retinoblastoma is often associated with subretinal fluid; the exudative retinal detachment can mimic the appearance of Coats disease.
Diffuse infiltrating retinoblastoma is usually unilateral and nonhereditary. It is found in children older than 5 years. The tumor presents with conjunctival injection, anterior chamber seeds, pseudohypopyon, large clumps of vitreous cells, and retinal infiltration of the tumor. There is no nodular growth pattern for retinoblastoma; however, uveal melanoma metastatic to the liver may exhibit a nodular or infiltrative pattern.

pool.q: A 5-year-old boy is found to have unilateral telangiectatic retinal vessels with an exudative retinal detachment. What histologic findings are characteristic of the likely diagnosis?

options.a: focal sclerosis of retinal vessels with an overlying pocket of liquefied vitreous
options.b: dilated, thin-walled vascular channels between the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and outer aspect of Bruch membrane
options.d: loss of capillary pericytes and thickening of the retinal capillary basement membrane

pool.rationale:
Coats disease is clinically evident within the first decade of life and is more common in boys. It is characterized by a unilateral retinal telangiectasia with mild to severe leakage and possible exudative retinal detachment. Foamy histiocytes and cholesterol crystals in the subretinal space are common histologic findings.
Loss of capillary pericytes and thickening of the retinal capillary basement membrane can be seen in diabetic retinopathy. Dilated, thin-walled vascular channels between the RPE and the outer aspect of Bruch membrane are found in polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy. Focal sclerosis of retinal vessels with an overlying pocket of liquefied vitreous is found in lattice degeneration.

pool.q: What structure is indicated by the arrow (figure)?

options.a: thinning of the corneal stroma with lipid exudation
options.c: linear pattern of inflammatory cells on the endothelium

pool.rationale: The photograph depicts a posterior embryotoxon, which appears as a thin, gray-white, arcuate line on the inner surface of the cornea. Anatomically, it signifies an anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line, which is the junction between the Descemet membrane and the trabecular meshwork. A posterior embryotoxon may occur as an isolated finding, or it may be seen in conjunction with ocular anomalies like Axenfeld-Rieger and Alagille syndromes. When the posterior embryotoxon is observed, it is important to look for other ocular abnormalities including fine peripheral iris strands to Schwalbe line (seen in the photograph), iris stromal hypoplasia, and glaucoma. Multilayered endothelial cells can be seen in posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy and in iridocorneal endothelial syndrome and can be demonstrated histologically or via confocal microscopy. Thinning of the corneal stroma with lipid exudation would be seen in Terrien marginal degeneration. A linear pattern of inflammatory cells on the endothelium (Khodadoust line) can be seen during episodes of corneal graft rejection.

pool.q: A 9-year-old child with a history of recurrent bacterial infections develops an intractable respiratory infection that proves fatal. The ocular and histopathologic findings of the patient are shown in the figure below. What is the most likely underlying disease in this patient?
pool.rationale:
The ocular findings as shown in the above figure, iris transillumination defects, fundus hypopigmentation, and decreased melanin distribution in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choroidal tissue are consistent with ocular albinism. Two notable syndromes associated with ocular-cutaneous albinism are Chédiak-Higashi syndrome and Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome.
Chédiak-Higashi syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder with a mutation in a lysosomal trafficking regulator protein that renders inadequate phagocytosis. This results in recurrent pyogenic infections, often involving the respiratory and cutaneous systems. Patients with Chédiak-Higashi syndrome rarely survive past 10 years of age and often succumb to infection. Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by ocular-cutaneous albinism and bleeding problems from a platelet abnormality. Gaucher disease is an autosomal recessive inherited disorder of metabolism involving glucocerebroside. Gaucher disease is not associated with albinism. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC) is a rare progressive genetic disorder characterized by an inability of the body to transport cholesterol and other fatty substances (lipids) inside of cells.
